questions.question: Light-headedness and one episode of almost blacking out bring a 65-year-old man to the emergency department. He has had diabetes mellitus for years and is known to have coronary artery disease. His monitor shows a slow rhythm made up of broad QRS complexes. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate as the most appropriate?
questions.explanation: A bradycardia that is producing symptoms of poor perfusion, such as near-syncope, and that carries a wide QRS suggesting block below the AV node, is an indication to capture the heart electrically. Transcutaneous pacing restores an adequate rate immediately while definitive therapy is arranged.

explanations.A: Amiodarone belongs to the tachyarrhythmia toolkit. Given to a patient who is already too slow, it depresses conduction further and can push the rate down towards asystole.
explanations.B: A bradycardia that is producing symptoms of poor perfusion, such as near-syncope, and that carries a wide QRS suggesting block below the AV node, is an indication to capture the heart electrically. Transcutaneous pacing restores an adequate rate immediately while definitive therapy is arranged.
explanations.C: Anticoagulation lowers clot risk but does nothing about a failing conduction system, and simply watching a patient who is already fainting allows the rhythm to deteriorate before help is given.
explanations.D: Atropine is the opening drug in symptomatic bradycardia, yet its vagolytic action works at the AV node. In high-grade, infranodal block with wide complexes it usually fails, so the algorithm moves on to pacing.

questions.question: A Tuohy needle is advanced through the interspinous ligaments until the plunger of a saline-filled syringe suddenly gives way, indicating that the tip lies in the potential space just outside the dura. A fine catheter is then threaded through the needle so that the drug can be topped up during labour. Which technique has been performed?
questions.explanation: The blunt Tuohy needle, the loss-of-resistance endpoint and the indwelling catheter for repeated or continuous dosing together identify the epidural route.

explanations.A: A subdural block is an unintended, poorly predictable spread of drug between dura and arachnoid. It is a recognised complication rather than a technique anyone sets out to perform.
explanations.B: In a spinal block a fine needle is deliberately passed through the dura until cerebrospinal fluid drips back; the drug is given as a single shot and no catheter is normally left behind.
explanations.C: The blunt Tuohy needle, the loss-of-resistance endpoint and the indwelling catheter for repeated or continuous dosing together identify the epidural route.
explanations.D: General anaesthesia depends on intravenous or inhaled agents and control of the airway, so no needle is placed in the back at all.

questions.question: Some weeks after being injured in a road traffic accident, a patient complains of constant burning and shooting, electric shock-like pain in the affected limb, with the skin unusually sensitive to light touch. Which drug is the most appropriate choice for this kind of pain?
questions.explanation: Gabapentin binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of neuronal calcium channels and damps down the abnormal discharge from injured nerves. Together with pregabalin, tricyclic antidepressants and SNRIs such as duloxetine, it is standard first-line therapy for neuropathic pain.

explanations.A: Paracetamol works centrally on ordinary nociceptive pain of mild degree. It has no effect on the ectopic firing of damaged nerves and gives little relief in neuropathic states.
explanations.B: Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs suppress prostaglandin-driven inflammatory pain. Where the lesion lies in the nerve itself, this mechanism is largely irrelevant.
explanations.C: Tramadol combines weak mu-agonism with reuptake inhibition of noradrenaline and serotonin, so it does help somewhat, but guidelines place it as a second-line or add-on agent rather than the drug of choice.
explanations.D: Gabapentin binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of neuronal calcium channels and damps down the abnormal discharge from injured nerves. Together with pregabalin, tricyclic antidepressants and SNRIs such as duloxetine, it is standard first-line therapy for neuropathic pain.

questions.question: A woman on long-term treatment for rheumatoid arthritis was hospitalised in the past for a gastric ulcer. Considering that history, which of the following drugs would be the most suitable for controlling her joint disease?
questions.explanation: Celecoxib spares COX-1, the isoform that maintains the protective gastric mucus and bicarbonate layer, so it delivers anti-inflammatory benefit with markedly fewer ulcers and bleeds. That makes it the preferred NSAID when peptic ulcer disease is in the history.

explanations.A: Celecoxib spares COX-1, the isoform that maintains the protective gastric mucus and bicarbonate layer, so it delivers anti-inflammatory benefit with markedly fewer ulcers and bleeds. That makes it the preferred NSAID when peptic ulcer disease is in the history.
explanations.B: Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist used to reverse respiratory depression. It has neither analgesic nor anti-inflammatory activity and no place in arthritis.
explanations.C: Paracetamol is gastric-friendly but barely anti-inflammatory, so it cannot control the synovitis that drives joint destruction in rheumatoid arthritis.
explanations.D: Ibuprofen blocks COX-1 as well as COX-2 and would clearly raise the chance of ulcer recurrence and gastrointestinal haemorrhage in a patient already sensitised.

questions.question: After several hours outdoors during a heat wave, an elderly man collapses and is diagnosed with heat stroke. Which one of the following findings would you NOT expect to see in him?
questions.explanation: This is the exception. In classic non-exertional heat stroke the hypothalamic set point and the sweating response have failed, so the patient stops perspiring (anhidrosis) even as the core temperature climbs. Profuse sweating belongs to heat exhaustion, not heat stroke.

explanations.A: This is the exception. In classic non-exertional heat stroke the hypothalamic set point and the sweating response have failed, so the patient stops perspiring (anhidrosis) even as the core temperature climbs. Profuse sweating belongs to heat exhaustion, not heat stroke.
explanations.B: Marked hyperthermia is the rule; the formal diagnostic threshold is a core temperature above 40°C (104°F), and a reading of 103°F sits squarely in the abnormal, high range, so it is not the odd finding out.
explanations.C: Tachycardia is expected. Cutaneous vasodilatation and dehydration reduce effective circulating volume, and cardiac output rises steeply in an attempt to shed heat.
explanations.D: Skin that is hot, dry and flushed is the textbook picture, and it follows directly from the failure of sweating combined with maximal skin vasodilatation.

questions.question: An adult supported on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation remains in respiratory distress although the ventilator and pump settings have been verified as adequate. What should the nurse do next?
questions.explanation: When the prescribed settings are correct but the patient is not improving, the fault usually lies in the circuit. Inspecting for a kinked line, clot or fibrin deposit in the oxygenator, cannula migration or chatter caused by inadequate drainage identifies a mechanical problem that no amount of dial-turning will fix.

explanations.A: Pushing up tidal volume works against the lung-rest strategy that ECMO exists to provide and exposes already injured alveoli to volutrauma, all without touching the reason for the distress.
explanations.B: When the prescribed settings are correct but the patient is not improving, the fault usually lies in the circuit. Inspecting for a kinked line, clot or fibrin deposit in the oxygenator, cannula migration or chatter caused by inadequate drainage identifies a mechanical problem that no amount of dial-turning will fix.
explanations.C: Raising flow blindly increases shear stress and haemolysis and may simply mask an obstruction that is still worsening.
explanations.D: Turning the sweep or FiO2 to 100% adds oxygen toxicity risk and buys only a brief cosmetic improvement if the real problem is a failing circuit.

questions.question: An adult in cardiac arrest is found to be in ventricular fibrillation and defibrillation is under way. At which point in the shock sequence is the first dose of adrenaline given, and how much is given?
questions.explanation: In a shockable rhythm defibrillation takes priority, because early shocks are what actually terminate ventricular fibrillation. Adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO is therefore given once the third shock has failed, and repeated every 3 to 5 minutes thereafter alongside uninterrupted compressions.

explanations.A: Adult adrenaline is prescribed in milligrams, not in millilitres of an undefined dilution; 0.1 mL-type volumes belong to weight-based paediatric dosing.
explanations.B: Both parts are wrong here: the adult dose is 1 mg of 1:10,000 solution intravenously or intraosseously, and in a shockable rhythm the drug is deliberately held back until the initial shocks have had their chance.
explanations.C: In a shockable rhythm defibrillation takes priority, because early shocks are what actually terminate ventricular fibrillation. Adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO is therefore given once the third shock has failed, and repeated every 3 to 5 minutes thereafter alongside uninterrupted compressions.
explanations.D: The 1 mg dose is correct, but giving it after the second shock is too early in a shockable rhythm; that early timing applies to non-shockable arrest, where adrenaline is given as soon as access is obtained.

questions.question: Failure of the outflow foramina of the fourth ventricle, namely the foramina of Luschka and Magendie, to open normally is the underlying defect in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Atresia of the lateral and median apertures traps cerebrospinal fluid inside the fourth ventricle, which balloons into a posterior fossa cyst. The associated hypoplasia or agenesis of the cerebellar vermis, with an enlarged posterior fossa and raised tentorium, completes the Dandy-Walker picture.

explanations.A: Atresia of the lateral and median apertures traps cerebrospinal fluid inside the fourth ventricle, which balloons into a posterior fossa cyst. The associated hypoplasia or agenesis of the cerebellar vermis, with an enlarged posterior fossa and raised tentorium, completes the Dandy-Walker picture.
explanations.B: In Chiari malformation the cerebellar tonsils and part of the medulla are displaced downwards through the foramen magnum; the apertures themselves are formed, and hydrocephalus arises from crowding at the craniovertebral junction.
explanations.C: Aqueductal stenosis narrows the cerebral aqueduct linking the third and fourth ventricles, so the fourth ventricle stays small while the ones above it dilate, exactly the reverse of the Dandy-Walker pattern.
explanations.D: Spina bifida is a defect of posterior neural tube closure over the spine. It may accompany a Chiari II malformation, but it is not a disorder of fourth-ventricular outflow.

questions.question: Among the drugs used in the standard first-line regimen for tuberculosis, which one is considered to have the greatest bactericidal power against the tubercle bacillus?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin blocks DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and kills bacilli wherever they sit, whether multiplying briskly in cavities, lying semi-dormant in caseous foci or hiding inside macrophages. This breadth of killing, plus its powerful sterilising effect that permits short-course therapy, is why it is ranked the most bactericidal of the first-line drugs.

explanations.A: Rifampicin blocks DNA-dependent RNA polymerase and kills bacilli wherever they sit, whether multiplying briskly in cavities, lying semi-dormant in caseous foci or hiding inside macrophages. This breadth of killing, plus its powerful sterilising effect that permits short-course therapy, is why it is ranked the most bactericidal of the first-line drugs.
explanations.B: Ethambutol inhibits arabinosyl transferase and is essentially bacteriostatic at usual doses. It is added mainly to protect the companion drugs against emerging resistance.
explanations.C: Isoniazid is strongly cidal against rapidly dividing extracellular bacilli and in fact shows the highest early bactericidal activity in the first two days of treatment, but its reach into slow-growing and intracellular populations is narrower than that of rifampicin.
explanations.D: Pyrazinamide comes into its own only in the acidic environment inside macrophages and inflamed lesions, killing the persisters that shorten therapy. Outside that niche it is largely inactive, so it is not the most bactericidal drug overall.

questions.question: A metered dose inhaler is dispensed with 200 doses in the canister. The prescription reads two puffs every six hours. Roughly how many days will a single inhaler last?
questions.explanation: A six-hourly order means four doses in 24 hours. Four doses of two puffs comes to 8 puffs each day, and 200 divided by 8 gives exactly 25 days.

explanations.A: Twenty days at 8 puffs a day accounts for only 160 actuations, leaving 40 unused in the canister, so the inhaler has not yet run out.
explanations.B: A six-hourly order means four doses in 24 hours. Four doses of two puffs comes to 8 puffs each day, and 200 divided by 8 gives exactly 25 days.
explanations.C: Twenty-eight days would demand 224 puffs, which is 24 more than the canister holds.
explanations.D: Thirty days would need 240 puffs, well beyond the 200 supplied, so the patient would be inhaling propellant only.

questions.question: A nurse is reviewing the safe ways of giving calcium gluconate. Which one of the following methods of administration must be avoided for this drug?
questions.explanation: A rapid bolus floods the myocardium with calcium and provokes bradycardia, flushing, hypotension and, at worst, arrest in systole. The risk is greatest in a digitalised patient, so calcium is never pushed fast, and the ECG is watched while it runs.

explanations.A: A rapid bolus floods the myocardium with calcium and provokes bradycardia, flushing, hypotension and, at worst, arrest in systole. The risk is greatest in a digitalised patient, so calcium is never pushed fast, and the ECG is watched while it runs.
explanations.B: A slow, diluted intravenous push spread over roughly 5 to 10 minutes is the accepted way to stabilise the myocardium in hyperkalaemia or to abort tetany.
explanations.C: For symptomatic hypocalcaemia the drug is diluted in dextrose or saline and infused over 30 to 60 minutes, which keeps the plasma level rising gently.
explanations.D: Oral calcium salts are entirely appropriate for maintenance and for chronic hypocalcaemia once the emergency has passed.

questions.question: Cardiopulmonary resuscitation is in progress on an adult and an advanced airway has just been secured. While compressions continue without pause, how many ventilations per minute should be delivered?
questions.explanation: Once a tracheal tube or supraglottic device is in place the cycles of 30:2 are abandoned. One breath is delivered every 6 seconds, which works out to 10 per minute, while chest compressions carry on continuously at 100 to 120 per minute. Anything faster raises intrathoracic pressure and cuts venous return.

explanations.A: Once a tracheal tube or supraglottic device is in place the cycles of 30:2 are abandoned. One breath is delivered every 6 seconds, which works out to 10 per minute, while chest compressions carry on continuously at 100 to 120 per minute. Anything faster raises intrathoracic pressure and cuts venous return.
explanations.B: Twelve per minute, or one every 5 seconds, is the rate for rescue breathing in a patient who has a pulse but is not breathing adequately, not for CPR with compressions.
explanations.C: A rate near 20 to 30 per minute, one breath every 2 to 3 seconds, is the paediatric and neonatal recommendation with an advanced airway and is far too fast for an adult.
explanations.D: Six per minute would under-ventilate an adult in arrest; the 6-second figure refers to the interval between breaths, not to the number of breaths per minute.

questions.question: For a patient with extensive burns, the Parkland formula gives a total crystalloid requirement of 4800 mL for the first 24 hours counted from the time of injury. What volume should be infused during the first 8 hours?
questions.explanation: Parkland front-loads the fluid: half of the 24-hour volume goes in during the first 8 hours after the burn, and the remaining half over the following 16 hours. Half of 4800 mL is 2400 mL, given as warmed Ringer lactate and then titrated against a urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/hour in adults.

explanations.A: 1200 mL is one quarter of the total. Delivering only that much in the period of maximum capillary leak leaves the patient under-resuscitated and invites burn shock and acute kidney injury.
explanations.B: Parkland front-loads the fluid: half of the 24-hour volume goes in during the first 8 hours after the burn, and the remaining half over the following 16 hours. Half of 4800 mL is 2400 mL, given as warmed Ringer lactate and then titrated against a urine output of about 0.5 mL/kg/hour in adults.
explanations.C: 1800 mL corresponds to neither half nor a quarter of the calculated volume and has no place in the Parkland schedule.
explanations.D: 3000 mL exceeds the 50 per cent allocation. Over-resuscitation causes oedema, worsens the depth of the burn and predisposes to abdominal and limb compartment syndrome.

questions.question: On inspection of the neck, the jugular venous pressure is found to be raised. This finding most commonly reflects which of the following underlying states?
questions.explanation: The jugular column is a bedside manometer for right atrial pressure. When the intravascular compartment is overfilled, right atrial pressure rises and the venous pulsation is visible high in the neck. The same mechanism explains the raised JVP of right heart failure, tricuspid disease, tamponade and constrictive pericarditis.

explanations.A: The jugular column is a bedside manometer for right atrial pressure. When the intravascular compartment is overfilled, right atrial pressure rises and the venous pulsation is visible high in the neck. The same mechanism explains the raised JVP of right heart failure, tricuspid disease, tamponade and constrictive pericarditis.
explanations.B: Fluid overload describes the clinical picture that results, and it does raise the JVP. It overlaps heavily with hypervolaemia, but the examiners intend hypervolaemia as the precise haemodynamic term, which makes this a weak distractor.
explanations.C: A low circulating volume reduces venous return, so the jugular veins collapse and the JVP falls; it is not raised.
explanations.D: Dehydration is one route to hypovolaemia and likewise lowers, rather than raises, the venous pressure.

questions.question: A patient is receiving intravenous heparin, and the laboratory reports the latest activated partial thromboplastin time as 85 seconds. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
options: Hold the next dose of heparin
questions.explanation: Heparin is titrated to keep the aPTT at roughly 1.5 to 2.5 times the control, about 46 to 70 seconds in most laboratories. A value of 85 seconds is above that window, so the patient is over-anticoagulated. The correct response is to withhold the dose, inform the physician, watch for bleeding and recheck the aPTT before restarting at a reduced rate.

explanations.A: Heparin is titrated to keep the aPTT at roughly 1.5 to 2.5 times the control, about 46 to 70 seconds in most laboratories. A value of 85 seconds is above that window, so the patient is over-anticoagulated. The correct response is to withhold the dose, inform the physician, watch for bleeding and recheck the aPTT before restarting at a reduced rate.
explanations.B: Increasing the dose when the result is already supratherapeutic compounds the bleeding risk and is the opposite of what the sliding scale requires.
explanations.C: Carrying on unchanged ignores a result that lies outside the therapeutic range and leaves the patient exposed to haemorrhage.
explanations.D: Vitamin K restores the synthesis of factors II, VII, IX and X and is the antidote for warfarin. Heparin is reversed by protamine sulphate, given roughly 1 mg for every 100 units of heparin still circulating.

questions.question: A bougie is kept ready on the difficult airway trolley. What is this device mainly used for?
options: To assist endotracheal tube placement in a difficult airway
To measure airway resistance during mechanical ventilation
To facilitate suctioning of tracheal secretions
To maintain airway patency during mask ventilation
questions.explanation: The gum-elastic bougie is a long, semi-rigid introducer with an angled tip. When only the epiglottis or the posterior cords can be seen, it is slid blindly beneath the epiglottis into the trachea, where tracheal clicks and distal hold-up confirm its position, and the tube is then railroaded over it.

explanations.A: The gum-elastic bougie is a long, semi-rigid introducer with an angled tip. When only the epiglottis or the posterior cords can be seen, it is slid blindly beneath the epiglottis into the trachea, where tracheal clicks and distal hold-up confirm its position, and the tube is then railroaded over it.
explanations.B: Airway resistance is derived by the ventilator from flow and pressure measurements; no separate device is passed into the trachea to obtain it.
explanations.C: Clearing secretions is the job of a soft suction catheter or a rigid Yankauer, both of which are designed with suction ports the bougie does not have.
explanations.D: Keeping the upper airway open during bag-mask ventilation is achieved with an oropharyngeal or nasopharyngeal airway plus correct head positioning and a jaw thrust.

questions.question: While a central venous catheter is being inserted, the patient abruptly becomes breathless and air entry is found to be reduced over one side of the chest. Which complication is most likely to have occurred?
questions.explanation: The pleural dome sits immediately deep to the subclavian and low internal jugular puncture sites. If the needle strays through it, air enters the pleural space and the lung collapses, producing exactly this combination of sudden dyspnoea, unilateral loss of breath sounds and a hyper-resonant percussion note. A chest radiograph after every insertion exists to catch it.

explanations.A: The pleural dome sits immediately deep to the subclavian and low internal jugular puncture sites. If the needle strays through it, air enters the pleural space and the lung collapses, producing exactly this combination of sudden dyspnoea, unilateral loss of breath sounds and a hyper-resonant percussion note. A chest radiograph after every insertion exists to catch it.
explanations.B: A haemothorax from arterial or venous laceration can look similar, but percussion is dull rather than resonant and the dominant picture is one of blood loss and shock.
explanations.C: Tamponade follows late perforation of the right atrium or ventricle by the catheter tip. It announces itself with muffled heart sounds, hypotension and distended neck veins, and breath sounds stay equal on the two sides.
explanations.D: Venous air embolism causes abrupt hypoxia, chest pain and sometimes a churning mill-wheel murmur, yet air entry remains symmetrical because the lung has not collapsed.

questions.question: As intracranial pressure begins to climb, which of the following appears EARLIEST?
questions.explanation: The first complaints come from stretched dura and traction on pain-sensitive vessels: a headache that is worst on waking and aggravated by coughing or bending, vomiting that may be effortless and unrelated to meals, and subtle changes in level of consciousness such as restlessness or drowsiness. These, with papilloedema and visual blurring, mark the early stage.

explanations.A: A slow, bounding pulse is one arm of the Cushing response. It appears only when compensation has been exhausted and herniation is close, making it a late warning.
explanations.B: Irregular breathing, whether Cheyne-Stokes, cluster or ataxic, signals brainstem compression and completes the Cushing triad. Like bradycardia, it is a terminal rather than an early sign.
explanations.C: The first complaints come from stretched dura and traction on pain-sensitive vessels: a headache that is worst on waking and aggravated by coughing or bending, vomiting that may be effortless and unrelated to meals, and subtle changes in level of consciousness such as restlessness or drowsiness. These, with papilloedema and visual blurring, mark the early stage.
explanations.D: Rising systolic pressure with a widening pulse pressure is the third component of the Cushing response, a late compensatory attempt to preserve cerebral perfusion against the rising intracranial pressure.

questions.question: Arterial blood gas analysis on a patient admitted with an acute exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease confirms respiratory acidosis. Which management step is most appropriate at this stage?
questions.explanation: Non-invasive ventilation delivered as BiPAP is the established first-line therapy for a COPD exacerbation complicated by hypercapnic respiratory acidosis. The inspiratory pressure augments alveolar ventilation so carbon dioxide is washed out, while the expiratory pressure offsets intrinsic PEEP and relieves the work of breathing. Early NIV lowers intubation rates, hospital stay and mortality.

explanations.A: Non-invasive ventilation delivered as BiPAP is the established first-line therapy for a COPD exacerbation complicated by hypercapnic respiratory acidosis. The inspiratory pressure augments alveolar ventilation so carbon dioxide is washed out, while the expiratory pressure offsets intrinsic PEEP and relieves the work of breathing. Early NIV lowers intubation rates, hospital stay and mortality.
explanations.B: Intubation and invasive ventilation are held in reserve for patients who cannot tolerate NIV, who have a depressed sensorium or unprotected airway, or who continue to deteriorate on a trial of non-invasive support. Choosing it first exposes the patient to ventilator-associated pneumonia and weaning difficulty that NIV avoids.
explanations.C: Intravenous bicarbonate does nothing about the alveolar hypoventilation that is generating the acidosis. It also liberates additional carbon dioxide, which diffuses freely across the blood-brain barrier and can deepen central nervous system acidosis while the arterial pH appears to improve.
explanations.D: Limiting fluid intake has no bearing on carbon dioxide retention. It is a measure for volume overload states and, if applied here, may only add dehydration and thickened secretions to an already obstructed airway.

questions.question: A patient undergoing haemodialysis is found to have a serum potassium of 6.8 mEq/L. Which measure should be carried out first to protect the patient from a fatal outcome?
questions.explanation: Intravenous calcium gluconate raises the threshold potential of the cardiac myocyte and restores the gradient between resting and threshold potential, protecting the heart from ventricular fibrillation and asystole within minutes. It does not lower the serum potassium, so insulin with dextrose, a beta-2 agonist and dialysis follow, but membrane stabilisation is always the first move in severe hyperkalemia.

explanations.A: Intravenous calcium gluconate raises the threshold potential of the cardiac myocyte and restores the gradient between resting and threshold potential, protecting the heart from ventricular fibrillation and asystole within minutes. It does not lower the serum potassium, so insulin with dextrose, a beta-2 agonist and dialysis follow, but membrane stabilisation is always the first move in severe hyperkalemia.
explanations.B: Restricting dietary potassium is a maintenance strategy that prevents the next episode. It cannot influence a serum level that is already in the arrhythmogenic range.
explanations.C: Loop diuretics depend on nephrons that still filter and secrete. In a dialysis-dependent patient with little or no residual urine output, furosemide produces no meaningful kaliuresis and simply delays effective treatment.
explanations.D: Reducing intravenous fluids has no acute effect on potassium concentration and may worsen perfusion. It addresses volume status, not the electrical emergency.

questions.question: Atropine is ordered as a pre-anaesthetic medication for a patient scheduled for abdominal surgery. What is the reason for giving this drug?
questions.explanation: Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist. Blocking muscarinic receptors on exocrine glands dries up salivary, bronchial and gastrointestinal secretions, which keeps the airway clear during induction and reduces the chance of aspiration and laryngospasm. It additionally blocks vagal reflex bradycardia triggered by traction on abdominal viscera.

explanations.A: Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist. Blocking muscarinic receptors on exocrine glands dries up salivary, bronchial and gastrointestinal secretions, which keeps the airway clear during induction and reduces the chance of aspiration and laryngospasm. It additionally blocks vagal reflex bradycardia triggered by traction on abdominal viscera.
explanations.B: The opposite is true. Antimuscarinic blockade relaxes gastrointestinal smooth muscle and slows peristalsis, which is why atropine is used as an antispasmodic and why it can contribute to post-operative ileus.
explanations.C: Atropine has no antibacterial or antiviral activity whatsoever. Surgical infection is prevented by antiseptic skin preparation, sterile technique and timed prophylactic antibiotics.
explanations.D: Atropine relaxes the detrusor muscle and increases sphincter tone, so it promotes urinary retention rather than diuresis. Post-operative bladder distension is a recognised anticholinergic complication.

questions.question: A man brought to the emergency department after a pelvic injury is also found to have sustained trauma to the scrotum and testis. Which nursing action takes priority?
options: Apply ice packs and reassurance only
Start antibiotics and send urine culture
questions.explanation: Pelvic fracture with scrotal or perineal bruising, blood at the external meatus or a high-riding prostate signals possible urethral disruption. Catheterisation is withheld until a retrograde urethrogram clears the urethra; if the bladder needs draining before that, a suprapubic cystostomy is the safe route.

explanations.A: Passing a catheter blindly across an injured urethra is the classic error in pelvic trauma. A partial tear can be converted into a complete transection, with later stricture, incontinence and impotence as the price.
explanations.B: Pelvic fracture with scrotal or perineal bruising, blood at the external meatus or a high-riding prostate signals possible urethral disruption. Catheterisation is withheld until a retrograde urethrogram clears the urethra; if the bladder needs draining before that, a suprapubic cystostomy is the safe route.
explanations.C: Ice and reassurance address scrotal swelling and pain but leave a possible urethral tear and retained urine undetected. Comfort measures cannot substitute for ruling out a tract injury.
explanations.D: Antibiotics and a urine culture may be needed later, but they neither identify nor protect against urethral disruption, and obtaining the specimen may itself require the catheter that must be avoided.

questions.question: Several observations are recorded in a patient receiving opioid analgesia. Which one is the most alarming and demands immediate intervention?
questions.explanation: A respiratory rate below 12 per minute is the hallmark of opioid-induced respiratory depression, caused by reduced sensitivity of the medullary centre to rising carbon dioxide. Withhold further opioid, stimulate and support ventilation, give oxygen and have naloxone ready, because the next step in this progression is apnoea.

explanations.A: Opioid-induced constipation affects almost every patient on sustained therapy because tolerance to the gut effect never develops. It is uncomfortable and needs a scheduled stimulant laxative and stool softener, but it is not an emergency.
explanations.B: Nausea and vomiting are common in the first days of opioid therapy from stimulation of the chemoreceptor trigger zone. Antiemetics control it and tolerance usually develops within a week.
explanations.C: A respiratory rate below 12 per minute is the hallmark of opioid-induced respiratory depression, caused by reduced sensitivity of the medullary centre to rising carbon dioxide. Withhold further opioid, stimulate and support ventilation, give oxygen and have naloxone ready, because the next step in this progression is apnoea.
explanations.D: Retention from increased sphincter tone is a genuine adverse effect that may need catheterisation, but it threatens comfort and renal function over hours, not life within minutes.

questions.question: The ventilator alarms on a patient in the intensive care unit: peak airway pressure has risen abruptly and oxygen saturation is falling. What should the nurse do first?
questions.explanation: A sudden climb in peak inspiratory pressure with desaturation points to something blocking the circuit, most often accumulated secretions or a kinked or bitten tube. Clearing the airway by suctioning is the first nursing action. The DOPE mnemonic guides the rest of the check: tube Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax and Equipment failure.

explanations.A: Raising the delivered oxygen concentration may buy a little time but leaves the mechanical obstruction in place. Peak pressure will stay high and the saturation will fall again once the reserve is used up.
explanations.B: A sudden climb in peak inspiratory pressure with desaturation points to something blocking the circuit, most often accumulated secretions or a kinked or bitten tube. Clearing the airway by suctioning is the first nursing action. The DOPE mnemonic guides the rest of the check: tube Displacement, Obstruction, Pneumothorax and Equipment failure.
explanations.C: A bronchodilator is appropriate when bronchospasm is the cause, indicated by wheeze and a raised peak pressure with a near-normal plateau pressure. It is given after the airway is confirmed patent.
explanations.D: The physician must certainly be informed, but the patient is desaturating now. The nurse performs the immediate rescue manoeuvre first and reports the event and the response together.

questions.question: Analgesia has to be planned for a patient who has a documented history of peptic ulcer disease. Which approach to pain relief carries the least risk for this patient?
questions.explanation: Withholding NSAIDs altogether is the safest plan. Paracetamol is the preferred first-line agent, with an opioid added for severe pain; if an anti-inflammatory is truly unavoidable, a COX-2 selective agent under proton pump inhibitor cover is used with informed caution.

explanations.A: Non-selective NSAIDs inhibit COX-1, stripping the mucosa of the prostaglandins that maintain bicarbonate secretion, mucus and mucosal blood flow. In a patient who has already ulcerated, this invites recurrence, bleeding and perforation.
explanations.B: Withholding NSAIDs altogether is the safest plan. Paracetamol is the preferred first-line agent, with an opioid added for severe pain; if an anti-inflammatory is truly unavoidable, a COX-2 selective agent under proton pump inhibitor cover is used with informed caution.
explanations.C: Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1 for the life of the platelet, so it damages the mucosa and impairs haemostasis at the same time. It is the most ulcerogenic option listed.
explanations.D: A proton pump inhibitor substantially reduces, but does not abolish, NSAID-related mucosal injury, and it gives less protection in the distal small bowel and colon. Since the question asks for the safest option, avoidance still outranks NSAID plus PPI.

questions.subject: Medical-Surgical
questions.citation: KDT Essentials of Medical Pharmacology, 8e

questions.question: A few hours after undergoing a lumbar puncture, a patient reports headache accompanied by dizziness. Which nursing measure is most appropriate at this point?
questions.explanation: Post-lumbar-puncture headache arises from continued leakage of cerebrospinal fluid through the dural hole, which lowers intracranial pressure and drags on pain-sensitive structures when the patient sits up. Keeping the patient lying flat, prone with a pillow under the abdomen, presses tissue against tissue at the puncture site and helps the leak seal; generous oral fluids and analgesia complete the care.

explanations.A: The cerebrospinal fluid specimen is dispatched at the time of the procedure and is a documentation matter. It contributes nothing to the patient's present symptom.
explanations.B: Post-lumbar-puncture headache arises from continued leakage of cerebrospinal fluid through the dural hole, which lowers intracranial pressure and drags on pain-sensitive structures when the patient sits up. Keeping the patient lying flat, prone with a pillow under the abdomen, presses tissue against tissue at the puncture site and helps the leak seal; generous oral fluids and analgesia complete the care.
explanations.C: The physician is informed if the headache is severe, persists beyond the usual period or is accompanied by fever, neck stiffness or neurological signs suggesting a blood patch or another diagnosis is needed. Simple positioning comes first.
explanations.D: Deep breathing exercises are useful for atelectasis, not for a low-pressure headache, and straining may transiently worsen the discomfort.

questions.question: Which adverse effect do patients on nitroglycerin report most frequently?
questions.explanation: Dilatation of meningeal vessels produces a throbbing, usually frontal headache, and it is the commonest complaint with every nitrate preparation. It tends to settle over days as tolerance to this effect develops, and paracetamol relieves it; patients are counselled not to abandon therapy because of it.

explanations.A: Nitrates lower blood pressure by venodilatation, and the baroreceptor response to this is reflex tachycardia. Bradycardia is not a typical nitrate effect and, when it appears with inferior wall infarction, it is a reason to withhold the drug.
explanations.B: Dilatation of meningeal vessels produces a throbbing, usually frontal headache, and it is the commonest complaint with every nitrate preparation. It tends to settle over days as tolerance to this effect develops, and paracetamol relieves it; patients are counselled not to abandon therapy because of it.
explanations.C: Nausea may accompany the hypotension or the headache but is distinctly less frequent than the headache itself.
explanations.D: Palpitations do occur through reflex sympathetic activation, particularly after a sublingual dose, but they are reported far less often than headache.

questions.question: Acute pancreatitis is suspected in a patient presenting with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back. Which laboratory result is most characteristically raised in this condition?
questions.explanation: Serum amylase and lipase are the diagnostic biomarkers. A value greater than three times the upper limit of normal, together with typical pain, satisfies the diagnostic criteria without imaging. Lipase is the better test because it is more specific to the pancreas and stays elevated for eight to fourteen days, whereas amylase rises early and falls within two to three days.

explanations.A: Serum amylase and lipase are the diagnostic biomarkers. A value greater than three times the upper limit of normal, together with typical pain, satisfies the diagnostic criteria without imaging. Lipase is the better test because it is more specific to the pancreas and stays elevated for eight to fourteen days, whereas amylase rises early and falls within two to three days.
explanations.B: Marked hypertriglyceridaemia is an important cause of pancreatitis rather than a marker of it, and it can even falsely suppress the measured amylase.
explanations.C: Transaminases climb when a gallstone obstructs the common channel, so they help identify a biliary aetiology, but they arise from hepatocytes and are not pancreas-specific.
explanations.D: A rising creatinine reflects acute kidney injury from third-space fluid loss and signals severe disease on prognostic scoring. It is a marker of complication, not of diagnosis.

questions.question: A breathless patient has arterial blood gases reported as pH 7.50, PaCO2 28 mmHg and HCO3 24 mEq/L. Which condition best explains this pattern?
questions.explanation: The pH is alkalotic, the PaCO2 is low and the bicarbonate is still normal, which defines an acute uncompensated respiratory alkalosis; the kidney has not yet had time to compensate. Pulmonary embolism is the classic cause, because dead-space ventilation and hypoxaemia drive tachypnoea that blows off carbon dioxide.

explanations.A: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease causes carbon dioxide retention, so the expected picture is a low pH with a high PaCO2 and a compensatory rise in bicarbonate. That is the mirror image of these values.
explanations.B: The pH is alkalotic, the PaCO2 is low and the bicarbonate is still normal, which defines an acute uncompensated respiratory alkalosis; the kidney has not yet had time to compensate. Pulmonary embolism is the classic cause, because dead-space ventilation and hypoxaemia drive tachypnoea that blows off carbon dioxide.
explanations.C: Air embolism can also cause sudden hyperventilation, but it is uncommon and requires a specific event such as central line manipulation or a neurosurgical procedure. Pulmonary embolism remains the far more probable explanation.
explanations.D: Hypoxia is a mechanism rather than a diagnosis. It stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors and produces exactly this gas pattern, but the question asks for the underlying cause, and embolism is the condition that generates it here.

questions.citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e

questions.question: An unconscious patient is brought to the casualty department after a road traffic accident, and cervical spine injury cannot be excluded. Which intervention should be undertaken as the priority?
questions.explanation: A rigid cervical collar supported by manual in-line stabilisation, with head blocks and straps on a firm surface, prevents any movement of an unstable vertebral segment. An unconscious patient cannot guard the neck or report pain, so immobilisation is applied on the mechanism of injury alone to avoid a secondary cord injury that would be irreversible.

explanations.A: An airway adjunct is certainly needed in an unresponsive patient, but every airway manoeuvre in suspected cervical injury is performed with the neck held still. Jaw thrust replaces head tilt-chin lift, and an assistant maintains manual in-line stabilisation throughout.
explanations.B: Intravenous access and fluid resuscitation belong to the circulation step of the primary survey and follow airway and spinal protection.
explanations.C: A neurological examination establishes the baseline Glasgow Coma Scale and any sensorimotor level, but assessment must never postpone the measure that prevents further damage.
explanations.D: A rigid cervical collar supported by manual in-line stabilisation, with head blocks and straps on a firm surface, prevents any movement of an unstable vertebral segment. An unconscious patient cannot guard the neck or report pain, so immobilisation is applied on the mechanism of injury alone to avoid a secondary cord injury that would be irreversible.

questions.question: A patient under follow-up for chronic kidney disease is found to have a low serum sodium level. Which nursing intervention is the most appropriate one to begin with?
questions.explanation: Isotonic saline is the accepted initial fluid when the hyponatremia is symptomatic and the patient is volume-depleted, for example after vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretic use or a salt-losing nephropathy. It replaces sodium and water together, so the correction is gradual and the risk of osmotic demyelination is low. The infusion rate and serum sodium must be monitored closely because a diseased kidney excretes a free water load poorly.

explanations.A: Isotonic saline is the accepted initial fluid when the hyponatremia is symptomatic and the patient is volume-depleted, for example after vomiting, diarrhoea, diuretic use or a salt-losing nephropathy. It replaces sodium and water together, so the correction is gradual and the risk of osmotic demyelination is low. The infusion rate and serum sodium must be monitored closely because a diseased kidney excretes a free water load poorly.
explanations.B: Restricting water is the mainstay when the hyponatremia is dilutional, as in the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion or in the fluid-overloaded chronic kidney disease patient who cannot excrete free water. Assessment of volume status decides between this and saline.
explanations.C: Hypertonic 3% saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatremia with seizures, obtundation or coma. It is given in small boluses with hourly sodium checks, correcting no more than 8 to 10 mEq/L in 24 hours.
explanations.D: Diuretics increase renal sodium loss and, with thiazides in particular, are a recognised cause of hyponatremia. They are used only for the volume-overloaded patient and never as the first response to a low sodium.

questions.citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e

questions.question: Vasopressin therapy is started for a patient diagnosed with central diabetes insipidus. What change in the urine should the nurse expect?
questions.explanation: Vasopressin acts on V2 receptors in the collecting duct and inserts aquaporin-2 channels into the luminal membrane, so water is reabsorbed down the medullary osmotic gradient. The dilute urine of untreated central diabetes insipidus, with a specific gravity below 1.005, concentrates towards the normal range while the daily volume falls and thirst subsides.

explanations.A: Persistently high urine output after adequate vasopressin points to nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, in which the collecting duct cannot respond to the hormone. In the central form the polyuria settles, which is exactly what the water deprivation test uses to distinguish the two.
explanations.B: Vasopressin acts on V2 receptors in the collecting duct and inserts aquaporin-2 channels into the luminal membrane, so water is reabsorbed down the medullary osmotic gradient. The dilute urine of untreated central diabetes insipidus, with a specific gravity below 1.005, concentrates towards the normal range while the daily volume falls and thirst subsides.
explanations.C: A fall in urine volume, often from many litres a day to near normal, is the most obvious sign that the replacement is working. No change would mean the drug or the diagnosis is wrong.
explanations.D: A further fall in specific gravity is the opposite of the therapeutic response and would suggest continued free water loss, over-hydration or an ineffective preparation.

questions.question: A patient has been prescribed a monoamine oxidase inhibitor. Which dietary constituent must be kept out of this patient's diet?
questions.explanation: Tyramine in food is normally destroyed by monoamine oxidase in the gut wall and liver. When that enzyme is inhibited, dietary tyramine reaches the circulation, enters adrenergic nerve terminals and displaces stored noradrenaline in a burst, producing the cheese reaction: severe throbbing headache, hypertensive crisis, and the risk of intracranial haemorrhage. Aged cheeses, fermented and cured meats, soya products, yeast extracts, pickled fish, overripe fruit and red wine or beer are the foods to be avoided.

explanations.A: Tyramine in food is normally destroyed by monoamine oxidase in the gut wall and liver. When that enzyme is inhibited, dietary tyramine reaches the circulation, enters adrenergic nerve terminals and displaces stored noradrenaline in a burst, producing the cheese reaction: severe throbbing headache, hypertensive crisis, and the risk of intracranial haemorrhage. Aged cheeses, fermented and cured meats, soya products, yeast extracts, pickled fish, overripe fruit and red wine or beer are the foods to be avoided.
explanations.B: Glucose is metabolised through glycolysis and has no interaction with monoamine oxidase or with adrenergic transmission.
explanations.C: Fructose is a simple sugar with no amine structure and no relevance to monoamine oxidase inhibition.
explanations.D: Lactose is a disaccharide of glucose and galactose. It is only a problem for the lactase-deficient patient and has nothing to do with these drugs.

questions.question: On assessment a patient is noted to have dilated pupils, a raised blood pressure and a rapid pulse. These findings are typical of which category of pain?
questions.explanation: Acute pain triggers the sympathetic stress response. Mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, tachypnoea, pallor and diaphoresis are the objective signs that support the patient's report, and they resolve as the pain is relieved and the injury heals.

explanations.A: Acute pain triggers the sympathetic stress response. Mydriasis, tachycardia, hypertension, tachypnoea, pallor and diaphoresis are the objective signs that support the patient's report, and they resolve as the pain is relieved and the injury heals.
explanations.B: In pain lasting beyond three to six months the autonomic response adapts and the vital signs return to normal. The nurse instead looks for fatigue, disturbed sleep, low mood, irritability and withdrawal from activity, and must not treat normal vitals as evidence that the pain is not real.
explanations.C: Neuropathic pain from nerve damage is described as burning, shooting or electric, often with allodynia and numbness in a nerve distribution. Its hallmark is the quality of the sensation rather than an autonomic surge.
explanations.D: Visceral pain from internal organs is dull, deep, poorly localised and often referred, and it can be accompanied by nausea and sweating. Classification by autonomic signs alone still identifies this presentation as acute pain.

questions.subject: Fundamentals
questions.citation: Potter & Perry's Fundamentals of Nursing, 9e

questions.question: What term describes the passage of fresh red blood through the rectum?
questions.explanation: Hematochezia is bright red blood passed per rectum, either alone or streaking the stool. The blood has had no time to be digested, so it usually originates below the ligament of Treitz, from haemorrhoids, fissure, diverticular disease, angiodysplasia or colorectal tumour. Brisk upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage can also present this way, and then the patient is shocked.

explanations.A: Hematochezia is bright red blood passed per rectum, either alone or streaking the stool. The blood has had no time to be digested, so it usually originates below the ligament of Treitz, from haemorrhoids, fissure, diverticular disease, angiodysplasia or colorectal tumour. Brisk upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage can also present this way, and then the patient is shocked.
explanations.B: Melena is black, tarry, offensive stool produced when haemoglobin is acted on by gastric acid and bacteria during transit. It indicates bleeding from the upper tract and needs roughly 50 to 100 mL of blood to appear.
explanations.C: Hematemesis is vomited blood, either bright red or altered to coffee-ground appearance, and always localises the source proximal to the duodenojejunal flexure.
explanations.D: Occult blood is present in quantities too small to alter the appearance of the stool and is detected only by a faecal immunochemical or guaiac test, which is why such testing is used for colorectal cancer screening.

questions.citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e

questions.question: While a patient is being repositioned, the chest tube is accidentally pulled out of the pleural space. Which nursing action should be taken immediately?
options: Immerse the tube end in sterile saline
questions.explanation: The open chest wound must be sealed at once, because atmospheric air is being sucked into the pleural space with every breath. The nurse covers the site with a sterile occlusive dressing such as petroleum gauze, secures it on three sides so trapped air can still escape rather than build up into a tension pneumothorax, then stays with the patient, monitors respiration and saturation, and summons the physician for reinsertion and a chest radiograph.

explanations.A: Placing the end under water is the correct response when the drainage system disconnects but the tube is still in the chest. It has no place once the tube is out of the patient, and reinserting a contaminated tube risks empyema.
explanations.B: The open chest wound must be sealed at once, because atmospheric air is being sucked into the pleural space with every breath. The nurse covers the site with a sterile occlusive dressing such as petroleum gauze, secures it on three sides so trapped air can still escape rather than build up into a tension pneumothorax, then stays with the patient, monitors respiration and saturation, and summons the physician for reinsertion and a chest radiograph.
explanations.C: Clamping is contraindicated in this situation and in general during transport or a leak. Trapping air within the pleural cavity allows pressure to rise, shifting the mediastinum and obstructing venous return.
explanations.D: Encouraging deep breaths before the wound is sealed only increases the negative intrapleural pressure and draws in more air, worsening lung collapse.

questions.subject: Fundamentals
questions.citation: Brunner & Suddarth's Textbook of Medical-Surgical Nursing, 14e

questions.question: Midway through endotracheal suctioning of a ventilated adult, the pulse oximeter reading falls from 94% to 88%. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.explanation: Withdraw the catheter at once, then hyperoxygenate with 100% oxygen through the ventilator or a bag-valve-mask and let the saturation recover before attempting any further pass.

explanations.A: Pressing on with suction while the patient is already desaturating deepens the hypoxia and can provoke vagally mediated bradycardia or arrhythmia.
explanations.B: Withdraw the catheter at once, then hyperoxygenate with 100% oxygen through the ventilator or a bag-valve-mask and let the saturation recover before attempting any further pass.
explanations.C: Raising the vacuum pressure only strips more tracheal mucosa and worsens the oxygen debt; it does nothing to correct the desaturation.
explanations.D: Informing the physician matters, but it follows rather than replaces the immediate act of stopping suction and re-oxygenating the patient.

questions.citation: Potter & Perry Fundamentals of Nursing 9e — oxygenation and airway suctioning

questions.question: A hospitalised adult passes a total of only 100 mL of urine across a full 24-hour period. Which term describes this level of output?
questions.explanation: The cut-off used in most Indian nursing texts places anuria at 100 mL or less per 24 hours, so a 24-hour total of 100 mL is reported as anuria.

explanations.A: Oliguria denotes an output below roughly 400 mL in 24 hours, or under 0.5 mL/kg/hour, which is well above the figure quoted here.
explanations.B: The cut-off used in most Indian nursing texts places anuria at 100 mL or less per 24 hours, so a 24-hour total of 100 mL is reported as anuria.
explanations.C: Polyuria is the opposite picture, with sustained output above about 3 litres a day.
explanations.D: A healthy adult voids roughly 1000 to 2000 mL each day, so this figure lies far outside the normal range.

questions.question: An order reads: infuse 1000 mL of intravenous fluid over 8 hours. The giving set in use delivers 15 drops per mL. At how many drops per minute should the nurse set the infusion?
questions.explanation: Volume multiplied by drop factor, divided by the total minutes: (1000 x 15) / (8 x 60) = 15000 / 480 = 31.25, so the drip is set at about 31 drops/min.

explanations.A: 42 drops/min is what the same volume over the same time would require with a 20 gtt/mL set, not a 15 gtt/mL set.
explanations.B: Volume multiplied by drop factor, divided by the total minutes: (1000 x 15) / (8 x 60) = 15000 / 480 = 31.25, so the drip is set at about 31 drops/min.
explanations.C: 25 drops/min corresponds to a 12 gtt/mL set running the same volume over 8 hours.
explanations.D: 18 drops/min would deliver barely half the ordered volume within the time allowed.

questions.question: A couple is being investigated for infertility and the woman is booked for a hysterosalpingogram. Counting from the first day of bleeding, on which cycle day should the nurse arrange the study?
questions.explanation: The correct window is the proliferative phase, roughly days 7 to 10 once bleeding has stopped and before ovulation occurs; day 8 sits squarely inside it.

explanations.A: Day 21 falls in the luteal phase, when an early conception could already be implanting and would be exposed to contrast and radiation.
explanations.B: Day 14 is around the time of ovulation, so a newly fertilised ovum could be present.
explanations.C: Day 3 usually still lies within the menstrual flow, raising concerns about retrograde spill of blood and endometrial debris.
explanations.D: The correct window is the proliferative phase, roughly days 7 to 10 once bleeding has stopped and before ovulation occurs; day 8 sits squarely inside it.

questions.question: At caesarean section the surgeon asks for a non-crushing obstetric clamp whose blades end in broad triangular fenestrated tips, and applies it to the angles of the uterine incision to control bleeding. Which instrument has been requested?
questions.explanation: Green-Armytage forceps hold the angles of the uterine incision during LSCS, securing the cut edge and limiting blood loss without crushing myometrium.

explanations.A: Green-Armytage forceps hold the angles of the uterine incision during LSCS, securing the cut edge and limiting blood loss without crushing myometrium.
explanations.B: Babcock forceps end in rounded hollow ring tips designed for delicate hollow structures such as appendix, ureter or bowel.
explanations.C: Allis forceps carry interlocking teeth along the tip and grip firmly but traumatically, so they are unsuitable for the uterine angle.
explanations.D: Kocher's forceps have transverse serrations plus a 1x2 tooth at the tip, intended for tough pedicles and fascia.

questions.question: During a laparotomy the scrub nurse passes a hand-held retractor with a single long, thin blade of even width that sweeps into a smooth right-angled scoop, used to hold the liver and other deep abdominal contents out of the operative field. Name the instrument.
questions.explanation: The Deaver retractor is the long, gently curved right-angled blade used to gain exposure deep in the abdomen, classically for the liver and the gallbladder region.

explanations.A: Doyen's retractor is the bladder retractor of caesarean section, with a short handle set at right angles to a broad curved blade that sits over the pubic symphysis.
explanations.B: The Deaver retractor is the long, gently curved right-angled blade used to gain exposure deep in the abdomen, classically for the liver and the gallbladder region.
explanations.C: Langenbeck's is a small L-shaped retractor whose short blade suits superficial wound edges rather than deep viscera.
explanations.D: Morris retractor has a wider, shorter curved blade than Langenbeck but lacks the long sweeping curve of a Deaver.

questions.question: A labour room nurse opens a sterile drape that carries a V-shaped cut-out at the end where the woman's legs are positioned, so that only the perineum is left exposed for a vaginal birth. What is this drape called?
questions.explanation: The obstetric V-drape is defined by its V-shaped leg opening, which isolates the perineal field during a vaginal delivery.

explanations.A: The obstetric V-drape is defined by its V-shaped leg opening, which isolates the perineal field during a vaginal delivery.
explanations.B: An episiotomy pack is an assembled set of instruments, sutures and dressings rather than a single fenestrated drape.
explanations.C: A perineal sheet is the smaller under-buttock drape placed beneath the woman to collect liquor and blood.
explanations.D: A caesarean drape is fenestrated over the lower abdomen for a transverse lower segment incision, with no leg opening.

questions.question: Continuous electronic fetal monitoring during labour suggests that the umbilical cord is being compressed. Which fetal heart rate change best fits this situation?
questions.explanation: Cord compression produces variable decelerations, which are abrupt in onset and recovery and differ from one another in depth, shape and their timing relative to contractions.

explanations.A: Cord compression produces variable decelerations, which are abrupt in onset and recovery and differ from one another in depth, shape and their timing relative to contractions.
explanations.B: Late decelerations begin after a contraction has started and recover after it ends, reflecting uteroplacental insufficiency.
explanations.C: Early decelerations mirror the contraction curve and arise from vagal reflex during fetal head compression.
explanations.D: Hypoxia is a physiological state that a tracing may suggest; it is not itself a named deceleration pattern.

questions.question: Labour is being induced with prostaglandins when the woman develops uterine hyperstimulation, with contractions that are excessively frequent and prolonged. Which drug is the most appropriate management?
questions.explanation: Terbutaline, a beta-2 agonist, is the standard acute tocolytic for prostaglandin- or oxytocin-induced tachysystole; the offending agent is withdrawn and the woman repositioned at the same time.

explanations.A: Calcium gluconate is the antidote for magnesium sulphate toxicity and has no role in relaxing a hyperstimulated uterus.
explanations.B: Magnesium sulphate is used for seizure prophylaxis and control in pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, not as the acute tocolytic of choice here.
explanations.C: Hydralazine is a vasodilator reserved for severe hypertension in pregnancy.
explanations.D: Terbutaline, a beta-2 agonist, is the standard acute tocolytic for prostaglandin- or oxytocin-induced tachysystole; the offending agent is withdrawn and the woman repositioned at the same time.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman has lost three pregnancies in a row, each in the first trimester. Imaging shows a structurally normal uterus, her blood sugar values are normal, and antiphospholipid antibody testing is positive. Which diagnosis best explains this history?
options: Recurrent pregnancy loss due to uterine anomaly
questions.explanation: Three or more consecutive early losses together with persistently positive antiphospholipid antibodies, meaning lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or anti-beta2-glycoprotein I confirmed on two samples at least 12 weeks apart, establish antiphospholipid syndrome.

explanations.A: Three or more consecutive early losses together with persistently positive antiphospholipid antibodies, meaning lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin or anti-beta2-glycoprotein I confirmed on two samples at least 12 weeks apart, establish antiphospholipid syndrome.
explanations.B: A structural cause is excluded by the normal uterine anatomy described in the scenario.
explanations.C: Normal glucose values argue against gestational diabetes, which in any case manifests later in pregnancy rather than as repeated early loss.
explanations.D: Pre-eclampsia is a disorder of the second half of pregnancy and cannot account for repeated first-trimester miscarriage.

questions.question: Under India's cancer screening programme, health workers are trained to swab the cervix with dilute acetic acid and watch for a colour change in the epithelium. This test screens primarily for which condition?
questions.explanation: Acetic acid turns dysplastic cervical epithelium white, and VIA is the low-cost mass screening method for cervical precancer and cancer used at primary care level in India.

questions.question: Some weeks into anti-tubercular treatment that includes isoniazid, a 45-year-old man reports that both his hands and feet feel numb and keep tingling. Which nursing action takes priority?

questions.question: A student nurse asks whether someone who has never received tetanus toxoid is nevertheless shielded by the high immunisation coverage in the surrounding community. Which reply is accurate?

Offers no protection, since tetanus does not spread from person to person
Protects only those who are themselves vaccinated
questions.explanation: This is correct. Tetanus follows contamination of a wound by Clostridium tetani spores that are ubiquitous in soil, dust and animal faeces, and it is not communicated from one person to another. Herd immunity operates only against diseases spread person to person, so tetanus is the classic exception. Every individual must be protected directly through toxoid immunisation and appropriate wound management.

explanations.A: There is no level of community coverage that will protect an unimmunised person from tetanus, because vaccinating neighbours does nothing to remove spores from soil and dust.
explanations.B: Even partial herd protection is impossible here. Herd immunity works by interrupting a chain of transmission between people; with tetanus there is no such chain to interrupt.
explanations.C: This is correct. Tetanus follows contamination of a wound by Clostridium tetani spores that are ubiquitous in soil, dust and animal faeces, and it is not communicated from one person to another. Herd immunity operates only against diseases spread person to person, so tetanus is the classic exception. Every individual must be protected directly through toxoid immunisation and appropriate wound management.
explanations.D: The statement is true in itself but sidesteps what was asked. It restates that active immunisation protects the recipient, without explaining why the unimmunised person derives no benefit from the coverage around them.

questions.question: A 4-year-old child has had fever for more than five days together with a rash and non-purulent conjunctival redness, and the team is investigating for Kawasaki disease. Blood vessels of which calibre are chiefly attacked in this condition?

Coronary dilatation or aneurysm is the complication that determines prognosis, which is why intravenous immunoglobulin plus aspirin is given within the first ten days of fever and echocardiography is performed at diagnosis and repeated during follow-up.

explanations.A: Large-vessel vasculitides such as Takayasu arteritis and giant cell arteritis involve the aorta and its principal branches. Takayasu does occur in young people, but its presentation is pulse deficits and bruits rather than the mucocutaneous features described here.
explanations.B: Correct. Kawasaki disease is an acute self-limiting vasculitis of medium-sized muscular arteries, with a particular predilection for the coronary arteries. Coronary dilatation or aneurysm is the complication that determines prognosis, which is why intravenous immunoglobulin plus aspirin is given within the first ten days of fever and echocardiography is performed at diagnosis and repeated during follow-up.
explanations.C: Small-vessel disease describes IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein purpura), microscopic polyangiitis and granulomatosis with polyangiitis, which present with palpable purpura, glomerulonephritis or pulmonary haemorrhage rather than coronary involvement.
explanations.D: Veins are not the target of the classical vasculitis syndromes. Kawasaki disease is defined by arterial wall inflammation.

questions.question: A newborn has received BCG at birth. After what interval should the injection site be examined to confirm that the child has responded to the vaccine?

questions.question: A nurse wants to describe what proportion of a community is living with a particular disease on one specified date. Which epidemiological measure serves this purpose?
questions.explanation: Correct. Point prevalence is all existing cases, old and new, divided by the total population at that specified time. It is the snapshot measure and is governed by both how many people fall ill and how long they remain ill, which is why it is the indicator used for planning services, beds and staffing.

explanations.A: Incidence counts only new cases arising in a population over a defined interval. It measures the force of onset of disease rather than the load of disease present at a moment in time.
explanations.B: Correct. Point prevalence is all existing cases, old and new, divided by the total population at that specified time. It is the snapshot measure and is governed by both how many people fall ill and how long they remain ill, which is why it is the indicator used for planning services, beds and staffing.
explanations.C: Mortality rate quantifies deaths in a population over a period. It says nothing about how many people are currently living with the condition.

questions.question: Which of the following statements holds true for inactivated (killed) vaccines?

They usually need booster doses to sustain immunity
They confer lifelong immunity with no boosters
They work only when given as a single dose
questions.explanation: Correct. Killed organisms cannot replicate in the host, so the antigenic stimulus is limited to what is injected and the resulting antibody response is weaker and shorter-lived than that from a live vaccine. A primary series of several doses is therefore needed to establish protection, followed by boosters to maintain titres. Adjuvants are often added for the same reason.

explanations.A: Boosters are in fact routine for this class. The immunising schedules for DPT, IPV, hepatitis B and rabies all build in repeat doses.
explanations.B: Correct. Killed organisms cannot replicate in the host, so the antigenic stimulus is limited to what is injected and the resulting antibody response is weaker and shorter-lived than that from a live vaccine. A primary series of several doses is therefore needed to establish protection, followed by boosters to maintain titres. Adjuvants are often added for the same reason.
explanations.C: Durable, sometimes lifelong immunity after one or two doses is characteristic of live attenuated vaccines such as measles or BCG, in which the organism multiplies and mimics natural infection. Killed vaccines behave differently.
explanations.D: A single dose of a killed vaccine seldom produces protective immunity; it primes the immune system, and subsequent doses generate the protective response.

questions.question: While counselling a family about affordable sources of protein, a nurse compares 100 g of each of the following items. Which one delivers the most protein?
questions.explanation: Correct. Soybean provides close to 43 g of protein per 100 g, the highest of any commonly eaten food, and its amino acid pattern is near complete. This combination of quantity and quality at low cost is why it is favoured for nutrition rehabilitation and for supplementary feeding programmes.

explanations.A: Pulses such as lentils supply about 24 g of protein per 100 g. They are a valuable and inexpensive source, though limited in the sulphur-containing amino acid methionine and best combined with cereals.
explanations.B: Correct. Soybean provides close to 43 g of protein per 100 g, the highest of any commonly eaten food, and its amino acid pattern is near complete. This combination of quantity and quality at low cost is why it is favoured for nutrition rehabilitation and for supplementary feeding programmes.
explanations.C: Egg contains roughly 13 g of protein per 100 g. Its protein has the reference biological value against which others are judged, but the amount per unit weight is modest because the bulk of an egg is water.
explanations.D: Rice yields only about 7 g of protein per 100 g and is also deficient in lysine. It is chiefly an energy food and must be paired with pulses to make an adequate protein meal.

questions.question: Under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, what is the unique health ID chiefly meant to accomplish?
options: To fund the cost of hospital admissions
To establish a universal health identity through which healthcare and health records can be accessed seamlessly
To maintain immunisation records and nothing more
To carry out real-time surveillance of disease outbreaks
questions.explanation: Correct. The Ayushman Bharat Health Account, or ABHA, is a 14-digit identifier issued free of cost that lets an individual link, store and share their health records across providers with consent. It is the identity layer of the digital ecosystem, which also includes the healthcare professionals and health facility registries, and its purpose is a longitudinal record that follows the patient between facilities.

explanations.A: Paying for hospitalisation is the function of PM-JAY, the insurance arm of Ayushman Bharat. The digital mission creates infrastructure rather than financial cover, and holding a health ID confers no entitlement to funds.
explanations.B: Correct. The Ayushman Bharat Health Account, or ABHA, is a 14-digit identifier issued free of cost that lets an individual link, store and share their health records across providers with consent. It is the identity layer of the digital ecosystem, which also includes the healthcare professionals and health facility registries, and its purpose is a longitudinal record that follows the patient between facilities.
explanations.C: Immunisation data are handled through U-WIN and Co-WIN. Vaccination records can be linked to ABHA, but confining its purpose to that misses the point of a lifelong health record.
explanations.D: Outbreak detection and reporting run through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme and the Integrated Health Information Platform, which are surveillance systems and not individual identity accounts.

questions.question: A nursing officer is asked to explain how inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) is prepared and given. Which statement about IPV is correct?
options: Injectable vaccine providing immunity against polio
Requires only a single dose for lifelong immunity
questions.explanation: IPV is injected - intramuscularly as a full dose, or intradermally as fractional IPV in the national schedule - and the inactivated virus induces protective humoral antibody.

explanations.A: The drops given at birth and during pulse polio rounds are OPV; IPV is never given by mouth.
explanations.B: IPV is the killed (Salk) preparation. The live attenuated product is OPV (Sabin).
explanations.C: IPV is injected - intramuscularly as a full dose, or intradermally as fractional IPV in the national schedule - and the inactivated virus induces protective humoral antibody.
explanations.D: One dose does not confer lifelong protection; a multi-dose course is required, with fractional IPV given at 6 and 14 weeks in India's Universal Immunization Programme.

questions.question: While teaching about what goes into a vaccine vial, a nurse is asked why an adjuvant is added. Which statement correctly describes the role of an adjuvant?
options: Enhance the immune response to vaccines
Prevent the vaccine from being effective
questions.explanation: Substances such as aluminium hydroxide, aluminium phosphate and AS04 hold antigen at the injection site and stimulate antigen-presenting cells, giving a higher and longer-lasting antibody titre from a smaller quantity of antigen.

explanations.B: Substances such as aluminium hydroxide, aluminium phosphate and AS04 hold antigen at the injection site and stimulate antigen-presenting cells, giving a higher and longer-lasting antibody titre from a smaller quantity of antigen.
explanations.C: An adjuvant contains no living organism; the pathogen-derived component is the antigen, which is a separate ingredient.
explanations.D: Adjuvants are included precisely because they raise efficacy, not reduce it.

questions.question: Of the first-line anti-tubercular agents listed below, which is bactericidal rather than merely bacteriostatic against Mycobacterium tuberculosis?
questions.explanation: Both isoniazid and pyrazinamide are bactericidal, each acting on a different bacillary population, so the combined option is the complete answer.

explanations.A: Ethambutol is tuberculostatic and is included largely to hold back emergence of resistance, not for rapid killing.
explanations.B: Isoniazid is genuinely bactericidal against rapidly multiplying extracellular bacilli, but it is not the only bactericidal drug offered here.
explanations.C: Pyrazinamide kills semi-dormant bacilli in the acidic intracellular and caseous environment, which is why it allows therapy to be shortened to six months - again correct but incomplete on its own.
explanations.D: Both isoniazid and pyrazinamide are bactericidal, each acting on a different bacillary population, so the combined option is the complete answer.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman bleeds heavily soon after vaginal birth and is referred from the PHC with postpartum haemorrhage. Which drug should the nurse prepare to give first?
questions.explanation: Oxytocin given intravenously or intramuscularly is the first-line uterotonic for both prevention (active management of the third stage) and treatment of PPH - it acts within minutes and has few contraindications.

explanations.A: Misoprostol is the fallback for settings where oxytocin cannot be stored cold or injected; it is not preferred when oxytocin is at hand.
explanations.B: Oxytocin given intravenously or intramuscularly is the first-line uterotonic for both prevention (active management of the third stage) and treatment of PPH - it acts within minutes and has few contraindications.
explanations.C: Tranexamic acid is a valuable adjunct if given within three hours of onset, but it does not contract the uterus and never substitutes for a uterotonic.
explanations.D: Ergometrine is second-line and is withheld in pre-eclampsia, hypertension and cardiac disease.

questions.question: A 25-year-old client describes a lasting wish to dress in women's clothing and says his inner sense of himself does not match the sex recorded at birth. Which term is being described?
questions.explanation: Marked correct in the examination key: transvestism means the persistent urge to cross-dress, and the key treats the emphasis on wearing women's clothing as the defining feature of this vignette.
