explanations.B: Marked correct in the examination key: transvestism means the persistent urge to cross-dress, and the key treats the emphasis on wearing women's clothing as the defining feature of this vignette.
explanations.C: Homosexuality describes the direction of sexual attraction and says nothing about gender identity or dressing behaviour.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man under assessment for schizophrenia shows disorganised thinking and says he hears voices keeping up a running commentary on whatever he does. Which of the following is a Schneiderian first-rank symptom?
questions.explanation: Schneider's first-rank symptoms include the thought-alienation group (insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting), audible thoughts, third-person and running-commentary voices, passivity phenomena and delusional perception.

explanations.A: Withdrawing from people is a negative symptom - common in schizophrenia, but not on Schneider's list.
explanations.B: Schneider's first-rank symptoms include the thought-alienation group (insertion, withdrawal and broadcasting), audible thoughts, third-person and running-commentary voices, passivity phenomena and delusional perception.
explanations.C: Blunted or flat affect is likewise a negative symptom rather than a first-rank one.
explanations.D: Visual hallucinations are uncommon in schizophrenia and should prompt a search for delirium, another organic cause or substance use.

questions.question: A 35-year-old taking an antipsychotic complains of an inner restlessness that keeps him pacing and unable to remain seated. Which adverse reaction does this describe?
questions.explanation: Akathisia couples a subjective sense of inner restlessness with visible fidgeting, pacing and inability to sit still; it emerges early, is dose-related, and is managed by reducing the dose and adding propranolol or a benzodiazepine.

explanations.A: Tardive dyskinesia appears after months to years of treatment as involuntary chewing, lip-smacking and tongue movements, not as an urge to move.
explanations.B: Akathisia couples a subjective sense of inner restlessness with visible fidgeting, pacing and inability to sit still; it emerges early, is dose-related, and is managed by reducing the dose and adding propranolol or a benzodiazepine.
explanations.C: Acute dystonia produces sustained, painful muscle spasm such as torticollis, trismus or an oculogyric crisis.
explanations.D: Drug-induced parkinsonism causes tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and a mask-like face - slowing rather than restlessness.

questions.question: A 50-year-old is left with burning, shooting pain along a nerve after an injury to it. Which drug is most commonly used for pain of this type?
questions.explanation: Gabapentin, like pregabalin, binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of neuronal calcium channels and damps ectopic firing; it is a standard first-line agent alongside tricyclic antidepressants and duloxetine.

explanations.A: Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs act on inflammatory nociceptive pain and give little relief in neuropathic pain.
explanations.B: Gabapentin, like pregabalin, binds the alpha-2-delta subunit of neuronal calcium channels and damps ectopic firing; it is a standard first-line agent alongside tricyclic antidepressants and duloxetine.
explanations.C: Paracetamol is a weak central analgesic suited to nociceptive pain and is ineffective here.
explanations.D: Opioids such as morphine are held back for pain refractory to first-line drugs, because of tolerance, dependence and adverse effects.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man is started on disulfiram as part of treatment for alcohol dependence. What is the single most important instruction before he goes home?
options: Increase fluid intake to prevent dehydration
Take the medication with meals to reduce side effects
questions.explanation: Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, so even hidden alcohol - mouthwash, cough syrup, tonics, aftershave, some sauces - lets acetaldehyde accumulate, producing flushing, throbbing headache, vomiting, tachycardia and hypotension that can be severe enough to be fatal.

explanations.A: Tea and coffee are safe; caffeine does not interact with disulfiram.
explanations.B: Disulfiram blocks aldehyde dehydrogenase, so even hidden alcohol - mouthwash, cough syrup, tonics, aftershave, some sauces - lets acetaldehyde accumulate, producing flushing, throbbing headache, vomiting, tachycardia and hypotension that can be severe enough to be fatal.
explanations.C: Extra fluid is harmless but addresses nothing specific to this drug.
explanations.D: Disulfiram is taken as a single daily dose and does not need to be timed with food.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman with borderline personality disorder shows rapidly shifting emotions and repeated impulsive acts. Which psychotherapy is considered the treatment of choice?
questions.explanation: Dialectical behaviour therapy, developed by Marsha Linehan for exactly this disorder, combines individual sessions with skills training in mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness, and has the strongest evidence for reducing self-harm.

explanations.A: CBT works on distorted thinking and helps in depression and anxiety, but it is not the specific first-line therapy for borderline personality disorder.
explanations.B: Dialectical behaviour therapy, developed by Marsha Linehan for exactly this disorder, combines individual sessions with skills training in mindfulness, distress tolerance, emotion regulation and interpersonal effectiveness, and has the strongest evidence for reducing self-harm.
explanations.C: Classical psychoanalytic work is lengthy and, apart from structured variants such as mentalisation-based therapy, is not the first choice.

questions.question: After roughly three months of low mood, a patient has more recently become unusually energetic, over-talkative and reckless with money and driving; bipolar I disorder is suspected. How is the present episode best labelled?
options: Bipolar I disorder with current manic episode
questions.explanation: A preceding depressive phase followed by a current episode of elevated energy, pressured talk and disinhibited, risky behaviour makes this bipolar I disorder, currently manic.

explanations.A: Major depressive disorder is excluded once a manic episode has occurred at any point in the illness.
explanations.B: A preceding depressive phase followed by a current episode of elevated energy, pressured talk and disinhibited, risky behaviour makes this bipolar I disorder, currently manic.
explanations.C: Generalised anxiety disorder is sustained worry and tension without any cycling of mood.
explanations.D: Bipolar II is diagnosed when the highs are hypomanic - shorter than a week, without marked functional impairment, psychosis or need for admission - which does not fit this picture.

questions.question: For several years a patient has felt persistently low, tired and hopeless, yet has never had a full major depressive episode. Which diagnosis fits best?
questions.explanation: Dysthymia, renamed persistent depressive disorder in DSM-5, is depressed mood on most days for two years or more (one year in children and adolescents), with features such as low energy, poor self-esteem and hopelessness.

explanations.A: Major depressive disorder needs discrete episodes lasting at least two weeks with five or more criterion symptoms, which this history explicitly lacks.
explanations.B: Dysthymia, renamed persistent depressive disorder in DSM-5, is depressed mood on most days for two years or more (one year in children and adolescents), with features such as low energy, poor self-esteem and hopelessness.
explanations.C: Bipolar II requires at least one hypomanic episode, and none is described.
explanations.D: Cyclothymia needs two years of alternating hypomanic and depressive symptoms that never reach full episode criteria.

questions.question: A 45-year-old receiving opioids for pain after surgery is found to be breathing 10 times a minute. What should the nurse be most concerned about?
questions.explanation: Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to rising carbon dioxide, so a rate under 12 breaths per minute signals opioid-induced respiratory depression. Withhold the next dose, rouse and stimulate the patient, give oxygen, monitor sedation score and saturation, and keep naloxone ready.

explanations.A: Opioids more often lower blood pressure, through vasodilatation and histamine release, than raise it.
explanations.B: Opioids blunt the brainstem's response to rising carbon dioxide, so a rate under 12 breaths per minute signals opioid-induced respiratory depression. Withhold the next dose, rouse and stimulate the patient, give oxygen, monitor sedation score and saturation, and keep naloxone ready.
explanations.C: Bradycardia rather than tachycardia is typical of opioid effect; a fast pulse would point to pain, hypoxia or withdrawal.
explanations.D: Opioids do not raise blood glucose to any clinically meaningful degree.

questions.question: Asked a direct question, a patient with schizophrenia gives a reply that keeps veering away from the point and never comes back to it. This abnormality in the form of thought is termed:
questions.explanation: Tangentiality: the answer sets off at an angle to the question and never returns, so the point asked about is never reached.

explanations.A: Flight of ideas is the rapid, pressured stream of mania in which each idea sparks the next through links that can still be followed.
explanations.B: Tangentiality: the answer sets off at an angle to the question and never returns, so the point asked about is never reached.
explanations.C: Thought blocking is an abrupt break in the flow of speech, the patient losing the thread in mid-sentence.
explanations.D: Loosening of associations, also called derailment or knight's move thinking, is a more severe breakdown in which consecutive ideas have no discernible link at all.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy admitted to the child psychiatry unit repeatedly breaks ward rules, bullies younger children and becomes physically aggressive whenever he is corrected. Conduct disorder has been diagnosed. Which nursing approach is central to his care?
options: Implement strict rules and regulations with consistent enforcement
Avoid setting limits to reduce confrontations
questions.explanation: A predictable, structured milieu with clearly stated rules, uniform enforcement by every staff member and pre-agreed consequences is the evidence-based behavioural strategy in conduct disorder. Consistency is what makes the limits therapeutic; inconsistent enforcement teaches the child that rules are negotiable.

explanations.A: Unrestricted expression without boundaries removes the external control that these children cannot yet supply for themselves, and impulsive or destructive behaviour escalates.
explanations.B: A predictable, structured milieu with clearly stated rules, uniform enforcement by every staff member and pre-agreed consequences is the evidence-based behavioural strategy in conduct disorder. Consistency is what makes the limits therapeutic; inconsistent enforcement teaches the child that rules are negotiable.
explanations.C: Withholding limits to avoid a confrontation is negative reinforcement of the disruptive behaviour: the child learns that aggression makes demands disappear.
explanations.D: Drugs have only an adjunctive role, targeting comorbid aggression, ADHD or mood symptoms. The primary intervention is psychosocial - behaviour modification, social-skills and anger-management training, and parent training.

questions.question: The negative symptoms of schizophrenia are conventionally remembered as a cluster of 'A' words. Which of the following, though a classic Bleulerian feature of schizophrenia, is NOT counted among those negative symptoms?
questions.explanation: Ambivalence, the simultaneous holding of opposing feelings or impulses towards the same object, belongs to Bleuler's four fundamental 'A's (associations, affect, ambivalence, autism). It is a disturbance of volition and thought rather than a deficit state, and it does not appear in the standard negative-symptom list of blunted affect, alogia, avolition/apathy, anhedonia and asociality.

explanations.A: Apathy, equivalent to avolition, is loss of drive to begin or sustain goal-directed activity and is one of the five recognised negative-symptom domains.
explanations.B: Alogia is poverty of speech and of speech content, reflecting reduced spontaneous verbal output; it is a core negative symptom.
explanations.C: Ambivalence, the simultaneous holding of opposing feelings or impulses towards the same object, belongs to Bleuler's four fundamental 'A's (associations, affect, ambivalence, autism). It is a disturbance of volition and thought rather than a deficit state, and it does not appear in the standard negative-symptom list of blunted affect, alogia, avolition/apathy, anhedonia and asociality.
explanations.D: Anhedonia is the reduced ability to anticipate or experience pleasure and is a well-established negative symptom.

questions.question: A woman in the 20th week of pregnancy attends the antenatal clinic and her haemoglobin is estimated. Under Anemia Mukt Bharat, a haemoglobin below which value would label her anaemic?
questions.explanation: Anaemia in pregnancy is defined by WHO and by Anemia Mukt Bharat as Hb below 11.0 g/dL, and the cutoff applies in every trimester. Severity is then graded as mild 10.0-10.9, moderate 7.0-9.9 and severe below 7.0 g/dL.

explanations.A: Anaemia in pregnancy is defined by WHO and by Anemia Mukt Bharat as Hb below 11.0 g/dL, and the cutoff applies in every trimester. Severity is then graded as mild 10.0-10.9, moderate 7.0-9.9 and severe below 7.0 g/dL.
explanations.B: Hb below 12.0 g/dL is the threshold for non-pregnant women aged 15 years and above, not for pregnancy.
explanations.C: Hb below 10.0 g/dL marks the beginning of moderate anaemia; a woman with Hb of 10.5 g/dL is already anaemic, so this value is not the diagnostic cutoff.
explanations.D: Hb below 13.0 g/dL is the cutoff used for adult men.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man with schizophrenia has been maintained on a typical (first-generation) antipsychotic for five years with good control of his psychosis. Over the past few months he has begun to smack his lips and thrust his tongue out involuntarily, and tardive dyskinesia is diagnosed. Which step takes priority?
options: Initiate Propranolol to control motor movements
Increase the dose of the current antipsychotic
Substitute with Trihexyphenidyl for symptom control
Decrease the dose of current antipsychotic or switch to an atypical agent
questions.explanation: The first move is to reduce or stop the typical antipsychotic and change to an atypical agent, clozapine carrying the lowest risk. Where drug-free treatment is not possible, VMAT2 inhibitors such as valbenazine or deutetrabenazine are the approved symptomatic options.

explanations.A: Propranolol is the drug used for akathisia, the restless inability to sit still. It has no established role in tardive dyskinesia.
explanations.B: Raising the dose of the offending drug suppresses the movements only briefly, because it masks them by further blocking dopamine receptors, and it makes the long-term dyskinesia worse.
explanations.C: Anticholinergics such as trihexyphenidyl relieve acute dystonia and parkinsonism but aggravate tardive dyskinesia and should be withdrawn when it appears.
explanations.D: The first move is to reduce or stop the typical antipsychotic and change to an atypical agent, clozapine carrying the lowest risk. Where drug-free treatment is not possible, VMAT2 inhibitors such as valbenazine or deutetrabenazine are the approved symptomatic options.

questions.question: A 38-year-old man tells the nurse that the family next door watches everything he does and is planning to harm him, and nothing will convince him otherwise. This fixed false belief is best described as:
questions.explanation: A persecutory delusion is the unshakeable belief that one is being spied on, conspired against, cheated or threatened with harm. It is the commonest delusional theme in schizophrenia and matches this presentation exactly.

explanations.A: A grandiose delusion is an inflated conviction of one's own power, wealth, identity or special mission, which this man does not describe.
explanations.B: A persecutory delusion is the unshakeable belief that one is being spied on, conspired against, cheated or threatened with harm. It is the commonest delusional theme in schizophrenia and matches this presentation exactly.
explanations.C: In a delusion of reference the patient believes that neutral events - a news bulletin, a song, strangers laughing - carry a private message meant for him. The theme here is threat, not personal reference.
explanations.D: A delusion of control (passivity) is the belief that an outside agency is directing one's thoughts, feelings or movements from within.

questions.question: A nurse teaches the mother of an infant with cleft lip and palate to use a specialised feeding bottle. The device has a long, soft, compressible teat with a slit valve at the tip and a one-way valve at its base, so that the caregiver can squeeze milk into the baby's mouth in rhythm with the baby's sucking when the infant cannot generate negative pressure. Which feeding device is being described?
options: A standard bottle with an enlarged teat hole
questions.explanation: The Haberman (SpecialNeeds) feeder is the device described: an elongated compressible teat holding a milk reservoir, a slit valve at the tip that can be rotated to three flow settings, and a one-way valve at the base that stops milk running back into the bottle. Because the caregiver, not the infant, generates the pressure, it suits babies with cleft palate, Pierre Robin sequence or a weak suck.

explanations.A: The Haberman (SpecialNeeds) feeder is the device described: an elongated compressible teat holding a milk reservoir, a slit valve at the tip that can be rotated to three flow settings, and a one-way valve at the base that stops milk running back into the bottle. Because the caregiver, not the infant, generates the pressure, it suits babies with cleft palate, Pierre Robin sequence or a weak suck.
explanations.B: The Pigeon cleft-palate bottle is also a specialty feeder, but it works differently - a Y-cut nipple that is firm on one side and soft on the other, so the baby compresses it against the intact gum ridge. Its short nipple is not squeezed by the caregiver.
explanations.C: 'Cleft lip/palate nurser' names a whole category of feeding equipment rather than the specific instrument described here.
explanations.D: Simply enlarging the hole in a standard teat floods the infant and raises the aspiration risk; it does not replace a valved cleft feeder.

questions.question: In India's newborn health programme, the abbreviation INAP expands to which of the following?
questions.explanation: INAP is the India Newborn Action Plan, launched in September 2014 as the country's response to the Global Every Newborn Action Plan. It commits India to a single-digit neonatal mortality rate and a single-digit stillbirth rate by 2030, working through six pillars from preconception care to care of the small and sick newborn.

explanations.A: INAP is the India Newborn Action Plan, launched in September 2014 as the country's response to the Global Every Newborn Action Plan. It commits India to a single-digit neonatal mortality rate and a single-digit stillbirth rate by 2030, working through six pillars from preconception care to care of the small and sick newborn.
explanations.B: The plan is officially titled with the word 'Newborn'; 'Neonatal' is not the term used in the document.
explanations.C: The second half of the title is 'Action Plan', not 'Active Plan'.
explanations.D: Both words in this option differ from the official title.

questions.question: A boot-shaped cardiac shadow, described as 'coeur en sabot' on a chest radiograph, is the classical appearance in which condition?
questions.explanation: In tetralogy of Fallot the hypertrophied right ventricle lifts the cardiac apex off the diaphragm while the pulmonary trunk is small, leaving a concave upper left border. Together these produce the upturned-apex, boot-shaped silhouette with oligaemic lung fields.

explanations.A: Tricuspid atresia is recognised by left axis deviation on ECG with a small or normal-sized heart; it does not give the classical boot contour.
explanations.B: In tetralogy of Fallot the hypertrophied right ventricle lifts the cardiac apex off the diaphragm while the pulmonary trunk is small, leaving a concave upper left border. Together these produce the upturned-apex, boot-shaped silhouette with oligaemic lung fields.
explanations.C: Truncus arteriosus gives a single great vessel with plethoric lungs and often a right aortic arch, not a boot shape.
explanations.D: Supracardiac total anomalous pulmonary venous return gives the 'snowman' or figure-of-eight silhouette produced by the dilated vertical vein and superior vena cava.

questions.question: The parents of an infant with eczema are given a topical corticosteroid cream. Which instruction should the nurse stress while counselling them?
options: Apply at night time to reduce systemic absorption
Gastric irritation occurs when hands are put in mouth
Causes hair growth at application site
Apply a thin layer only on the affected area and avoid prolonged use
questions.explanation: This is the essential counselling point. A thin film should be applied only to the affected skin for the shortest effective period, occlusive dressings and tight nappies should be avoided over treated skin, and only the mildest effective potency should be used on the face and flexures. Prolonged or extensive use in infants risks skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia and suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, because the infant's surface-area-to-weight ratio favours absorption.

explanations.A: The time of day makes no material difference to absorption. What governs systemic uptake is the potency of the preparation, the surface area treated, the thinness of the skin and the length of treatment.
explanations.B: Topical corticosteroids do not cause gastric irritation in the quantities a child might transfer to the mouth; the systemic hazards are adrenal suppression and growth effects, not gastritis.
explanations.C: Hypertrichosis can occur at the application site, but it is a minor cosmetic effect and not the key safety message.
explanations.D: This is the essential counselling point. A thin film should be applied only to the affected skin for the shortest effective period, occlusive dressings and tight nappies should be avoided over treated skin, and only the mildest effective potency should be used on the face and flexures. Prolonged or extensive use in infants risks skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia and suppression of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis, because the infant's surface-area-to-weight ratio favours absorption.

questions.question: Which scoring system or systems are used in the neonatal intensive care unit to grade the severity of respiratory distress in a newborn?
options: Both the Silverman-Anderson and the Downes score
questions.explanation: Both scores are in routine NICU use: Silverman-Anderson grades retractions, grunting and nasal flaring, while Downes adds cyanosis and air entry.

explanations.A: The Silverman-Anderson score grades five signs - upper chest movement, lower chest retraction, xiphoid retraction, nasal flaring and expiratory grunt - each 0 to 2 for a total of 10, and is favoured in preterm infants. It is correct but incomplete as an answer.
explanations.B: The Downes score grades respiratory rate, cyanosis, air entry, grunting and retractions, again 0 to 2 each, and is preferred in term and near-term babies; a score above 6 signals impending respiratory failure. Also correct but incomplete.
explanations.C: Both scores are in routine NICU use: Silverman-Anderson grades retractions, grunting and nasal flaring, while Downes adds cyanosis and air entry.
explanations.D: APGAR grades adaptation in the first minutes of life; it is not a respiratory-distress severity score.

questions.question: In a child developing raised intracranial pressure, which of the following features appears earliest?
questions.explanation: A change in level of consciousness is the earliest and most sensitive indicator. In young children it shows as irritability, an unusual high-pitched cry, refusal to feed, restlessness or drowsiness, and it precedes any change in pupils, blood pressure or respiratory pattern.

explanations.A: A change in level of consciousness is the earliest and most sensitive indicator. In young children it shows as irritability, an unusual high-pitched cry, refusal to feed, restlessness or drowsiness, and it precedes any change in pupils, blood pressure or respiratory pattern.
explanations.B: Headache is a genuine symptom but depends on the child being old enough to report it, so it is missed in infants and toddlers.
explanations.C: Vomiting, classically effortless and worse in the morning, follows the change in behaviour and consciousness rather than preceding it.
explanations.D: Seizures indicate advanced intracranial hypertension. Together with bradycardia, widened pulse pressure and irregular respiration (Cushing's triad) and pupillary changes, they are late and ominous signs.

questions.question: A child on high-flow nasal cannula therapy suddenly desaturates and the pulse oximeter reads SpO2 50%. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate at that moment?
options: Increase HFNC flow rate by 5 L/min
Call the Respiratory Therapist to adjust the FiO2
Immediately discontinue HFNC and switch to BVM with 100% oxygen
Reposition the child prone and reassess SpO2 after 15 minutes
questions.explanation: Critical hypoxaemia demands immediate positive-pressure ventilation with a bag-valve-mask on 100% oxygen with a reservoir, while help is called and the cause is sought. In paediatric emergencies effective oxygenation and ventilation take precedence over adjusting any oxygen-delivery device.

explanations.A: Adding flow only titrates a device that has already failed. At an SpO2 of 50% the child has minutes of reserve, and bradycardia followed by cardiac arrest is the next step in the paediatric deterioration sequence.
explanations.B: Summoning another professional before delivering oxygen delays rescue ventilation. The nurse at the bedside must ventilate first and call for help simultaneously.
explanations.C: Critical hypoxaemia demands immediate positive-pressure ventilation with a bag-valve-mask on 100% oxygen with a reservoir, while help is called and the cause is sought. In paediatric emergencies effective oxygenation and ventilation take precedence over adjusting any oxygen-delivery device.
explanations.D: A 15-minute wait at an SpO2 of 50% is indefensible; hypoxic bradycardia and arrest would occur long before the reassessment.

questions.question: During a home visit a mother complains to the nurse that her 4-year-old is not receiving supplementary nutrition from the anganwadi under ICDS. What should the nurse do first?
options: Refer to a pediatrician for evaluation
Verify the child's age and ICDS enrollment status
questions.explanation: The nursing process opens with assessment. The nurse confirms that the child falls within the eligible 6 months to 6 years age band and checks whether the child is actually registered at the anganwadi centre, since non-enrolment, and not denial of service, is the usual reason a child receives nothing.

explanations.A: A medical referral answers a clinical question that has not yet been asked. Nothing so far suggests illness; the complaint is about service delivery.
explanations.B: The nursing process opens with assessment. The nurse confirms that the child falls within the eligible 6 months to 6 years age band and checks whether the child is actually registered at the anganwadi centre, since non-enrolment, and not denial of service, is the usual reason a child receives nothing.
explanations.C: Nutrition education is a valid intervention but belongs after the assessment has defined the problem.
explanations.D: Handing out supplementary food before eligibility and enrolment are verified bypasses programme records, distorts the centre's beneficiary count and does not correct the underlying gap.

questions.question: A 2-month-old is brought with repeated vomiting and a rapidly enlarging head. The anterior fontanelle is tense and full and both eyes are deviated downwards with sclera visible above the iris (setting-sun sign). MRI shows a cystically dilated fourth ventricle with hypoplasia of the cerebellar vermis, and Dandy-Walker malformation is diagnosed. Which mechanism underlies the hydrocephalus?
options: Atresia of Luschka and Magendie → non-communicating hydrocephalus
CSF malabsorption by defective arachnoid granulations
questions.explanation: Dandy-Walker malformation results from failure of development of the outlet foramina of Luschka and Magendie, so cerebrospinal fluid cannot escape from the fourth ventricle. The trapped fluid balloons the fourth ventricle into a posterior fossa cyst, the vermis fails to form fully, and a non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus develops with an enlarging head, tense fontanelle and setting-sun eyes.

explanations.A: Stenosis of the cerebral aqueduct is the commonest cause of congenital obstructive hydrocephalus, but it dilates the lateral and third ventricles while leaving the fourth ventricle small - the opposite of the MRI finding here.
explanations.B: Dandy-Walker malformation results from failure of development of the outlet foramina of Luschka and Magendie, so cerebrospinal fluid cannot escape from the fourth ventricle. The trapped fluid balloons the fourth ventricle into a posterior fossa cyst, the vermis fails to form fully, and a non-communicating (obstructive) hydrocephalus develops with an enlarging head, tense fontanelle and setting-sun eyes.
explanations.C: Excess cerebrospinal fluid production is characteristic of a choroid plexus papilloma, which shows an intraventricular mass, not a cystic posterior fossa with an absent vermis.
explanations.D: Impaired absorption at the arachnoid granulations produces a communicating hydrocephalus, typically after meningitis or subarachnoid haemorrhage, and would not distort the vermis or the fourth ventricle in this way.

questions.question: A 5-year-old is brought with acute watery diarrhoea. Following the national diarrhoea-management protocol used in India's ICDS and IMNCI services, what dose of zinc should be given and for how long?
questions.explanation: Every child aged 6 months and above receives elemental zinc 20 mg once daily for 14 days along with low-osmolarity ORS. The full 14 days matter because zinc shortens the current episode and also lowers the risk of further diarrhoea over the following two to three months.

explanations.A: The 10 mg dose belongs to infants under 6 months, and even for them the duration is 14 days, not 7. Both parts of this option are wrong for a 5-year-old.
explanations.B: Every child aged 6 months and above receives elemental zinc 20 mg once daily for 14 days along with low-osmolarity ORS. The full 14 days matter because zinc shortens the current episode and also lowers the risk of further diarrhoea over the following two to three months.
explanations.C: A 15 mg dose for 10 days appears in no national or WHO protocol.
explanations.D: A 30 mg dose for 7 days is not a recommended regimen; the standard schedule is fixed at 20 mg for 14 days in this age group.

questions.question: At 1 minute of life a newborn has a heart rate of 120 beats per minute, irregular respiratory effort, some flexion of the limbs, a weak cry, and a pre-ductal SpO2 of 62%. What should the nurse do next?
options: Administer supplemental oxygen and monitor SpO2
Dry the newborn, provide warmth, and reassess after 30 seconds
questions.explanation: The keyed answer. Because the baby is breathing with a heart rate above 100 but has laboured, irregular respiration, the response is to attach the pulse oximeter to the right hand and titrate oxygen against the minute-by-minute targets rather than to ventilate. Note that the targeted pre-ductal saturation at 1 minute is only 60 to 65 per cent, so a reading of 62 per cent is already within range and oxygen should be given only if the saturation falls below target on continued monitoring.

explanations.A: Positive-pressure ventilation is triggered by apnoea, gasping or a heart rate below 100 beats per minute. This baby is breathing and the heart rate is 120, so PPV is not indicated.
explanations.B: The keyed answer. Because the baby is breathing with a heart rate above 100 but has laboured, irregular respiration, the response is to attach the pulse oximeter to the right hand and titrate oxygen against the minute-by-minute targets rather than to ventilate. Note that the targeted pre-ductal saturation at 1 minute is only 60 to 65 per cent, so a reading of 62 per cent is already within range and oxygen should be given only if the saturation falls below target on continued monitoring.
explanations.C: Chest compressions are started only when the heart rate stays below 60 beats per minute after 30 seconds of effective ventilation with a secured airway. Nothing here justifies them.
explanations.D: Warmth, drying and stimulation are the initial steps completed within the first 30 seconds; by 1 minute they have been done, and management now turns on the ongoing assessment of breathing, heart rate and saturation.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the ductus venosus in the fetal circulation?
options: Shunts oxygenated blood from umbilical vein to IVC
Links umbilical artery to portal vein for nutrient delivery
Allows blood flow from RA to LA through foramen ovale
questions.explanation: The ductus venosus carries well-oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein straight into the inferior vena cava, bypassing the hepatic sinusoids so that the most oxygen-rich blood reaches the heart and brain. It closes after birth and persists as the ligamentum venosum.

explanations.A: The channel joining the pulmonary artery to the descending aorta is the ductus arteriosus, which closes after birth to become the ligamentum arteriosum.
explanations.B: The ductus venosus carries well-oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein straight into the inferior vena cava, bypassing the hepatic sinusoids so that the most oxygen-rich blood reaches the heart and brain. It closes after birth and persists as the ligamentum venosum.
explanations.C: The umbilical arteries carry deoxygenated blood away from the fetus to the placenta; it is the umbilical vein, not the artery, that relates to the portal system, and the ductus venosus is the shunt that bypasses it.
explanations.D: Right-to-left flow across the interatrial septum occurs through the foramen ovale, a separate shunt that becomes the fossa ovalis after birth.

questions.question: A 6-week-old boy vomits forcefully after every feed, the vomit contains no bile, and he has begun to lose weight. A firm olive-sized lump is palpable in the right upper abdomen and peristaltic waves are visible crossing the epigastrium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: This is classic infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. It declares itself between 3 and 8 weeks of age, more often in first-born males, with non-bilious projectile vomiting, an insatiable appetite immediately afterwards, weight loss and the palpable pyloric 'olive'. The obstruction is above the ampulla, so the vomit contains no bile, and loss of gastric acid produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis that must be corrected before pyloromyotomy. Ultrasound confirms the thickened elongated pylorus.

explanations.A: Reflux produces effortless posseting or regurgitation soon after feeds, usually in a thriving baby. It never produces a palpable olive or visible gastric peristalsis.
explanations.B: Intussusception typically strikes between 6 and 18 months with paroxysmal colic, drawing up of the legs, a sausage-shaped mass and redcurrant-jelly stools, and the vomiting turns bilious rather than remaining non-bilious.
explanations.C: This is classic infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. It declares itself between 3 and 8 weeks of age, more often in first-born males, with non-bilious projectile vomiting, an insatiable appetite immediately afterwards, weight loss and the palpable pyloric 'olive'. The obstruction is above the ampulla, so the vomit contains no bile, and loss of gastric acid produces a hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis that must be corrected before pyloromyotomy. Ultrasound confirms the thickened elongated pylorus.
explanations.D: Duodenal atresia presents within the first day or two of life with bilious vomiting and the 'double bubble' sign on abdominal X-ray, and it is strongly associated with Down syndrome.

questions.question: On examining a newborn, the nurse notes that one foot is turned inward at the heel and points downward, and it cannot be brought passively to a neutral position. Which line of management should be undertaken first?
questions.explanation: The Ponseti technique is the accepted gold standard. The foot is gently manipulated and then held in a long-leg plaster changed weekly, typically over about five to six casts; roughly 80 percent need a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy for the residual equinus, after which a foot-abduction brace maintains the correction for several years. Best results come from starting in the first week or two of life while the tissues are still elastic.

explanations.A: Operative release is held in reserve for the minority of feet that remain resistant or relapse after a full course of casting and bracing; it is never the opening step in an untreated newborn.
explanations.B: True congenital talipes equinovarus is a fixed structural deformity of bone, joint and soft tissue. Unlike positional foot postures it will not resolve on its own, and waiting only makes the tissues stiffer and correction harder.
explanations.C: The Ponseti technique is the accepted gold standard. The foot is gently manipulated and then held in a long-leg plaster changed weekly, typically over about five to six casts; roughly 80 percent need a percutaneous Achilles tenotomy for the residual equinus, after which a foot-abduction brace maintains the correction for several years. Best results come from starting in the first week or two of life while the tissues are still elastic.
explanations.D: Stretching and exercises without serial immobilisation cannot hold the corrected position between sessions, so the deformity recurs. Physiotherapy has a supporting role only.

questions.question: In an area where malaria transmission is high, a 3-year-old is brought to the health centre with fever and chills of three days' duration. Working under the IMNCI protocol, what should the nurse arrange first?
options: Refer to a higher center without treatment
Perform rapid diagnostic test for malaria and treat if positive
Start antipyretics and observe for 48 hours
questions.explanation: National policy is parasitological confirmation before treatment: a bivalent rapid diagnostic test or a blood smear, then species-directed therapy — chloroquine with primaquine for confirmed P. vivax, and artemisinin-based combination therapy with single-dose primaquine for P. falciparum. Any danger sign converts the plan to a pre-referral dose plus urgent transfer.

explanations.A: There is nothing here pointing to a bacterial focus. Handing out antibiotics for undifferentiated fever in a malarious belt both misses the likely diagnosis and drives resistance.
explanations.B: Referral without any assessment or treatment wastes time the child does not have. Rapid diagnostic kits and antimalarials are stocked down to the sub-centre and ASHA level precisely so that confirmation and treatment can begin where the child presents.
explanations.C: National policy is parasitological confirmation before treatment: a bivalent rapid diagnostic test or a blood smear, then species-directed therapy — chloroquine with primaquine for confirmed P. vivax, and artemisinin-based combination therapy with single-dose primaquine for P. falciparum. Any danger sign converts the plan to a pre-referral dose plus urgent transfer.
explanations.D: Falciparum malaria can progress to cerebral malaria or severe anaemia within hours. Suppressing the fever and waiting two days simply removes the one warning sign the family was watching.

questions.question: Hyperglycaemia that persists along with failure to gain weight leads to a diagnosis of neonatal diabetes mellitus in an infant. Which therapy should be instituted at the outset?
questions.explanation: Neonatal diabetes reflects an absolute lack of circulating insulin, so insulin replacement is the immediate answer. A continuous intravenous infusion is usually preferred at first because it can be titrated in very small increments against frequent glucose readings in a baby of low body weight, and it is converted to a subcutaneous regimen once the infant is stable.

explanations.A: A sulfonylurea such as glibenclamide does have a place, but only later and only in the subset shown on genetic testing to have an activating KCNJ11 or ABCC8 mutation of the KATP channel. Glucose control has to be established with insulin while that result is awaited.
explanations.B: Neonatal diabetes reflects an absolute lack of circulating insulin, so insulin replacement is the immediate answer. A continuous intravenous infusion is usually preferred at first because it can be titrated in very small increments against frequent glucose readings in a baby of low body weight, and it is converted to a subcutaneous regimen once the infant is stable.
explanations.C: Feeding adjustments alone cannot supply the missing hormone. Restricting intake in a baby already losing weight adds starvation to the metabolic problem.
explanations.D: Untreated, the osmotic diuresis leads to dehydration, ketoacidosis and death. There is no role for watchful waiting once hyperglycaemia is confirmed.

questions.question: Grunting, flaring of the nostrils and indrawing of the chest are being graded at the bedside in a preterm baby with suspected respiratory distress syndrome. Which scoring system is designed for this purpose?
questions.explanation: The Silverman-Anderson retraction score grades five observations — upper chest movement, lower chest (intercostal) retraction, xiphoid retraction, nasal flaring and expiratory grunt — each from 0 to 2, giving a total out of 10. A rising score signals worsening distress; 0 means no distress and scores above 6 to 7 indicate impending respiratory failure needing ventilatory support.

explanations.A: Apgar rates the adjustment to extrauterine life at one and five minutes using heart rate, respiratory effort, tone, reflex irritability and colour. It says nothing about the severity of ongoing respiratory distress hours later.
explanations.B: The Silverman-Anderson retraction score grades five observations — upper chest movement, lower chest (intercostal) retraction, xiphoid retraction, nasal flaring and expiratory grunt — each from 0 to 2, giving a total out of 10. A rising score signals worsening distress; 0 means no distress and scores above 6 to 7 indicate impending respiratory failure needing ventilatory support.
explanations.C: The New Ballard score estimates gestational age from six neuromuscular and six physical criteria and is valid down to 20 weeks. It is a maturity tool, not a distress tool.
explanations.D: Dubowitz scoring likewise assigns gestational age, using a longer list of external and neurological signs; it has largely been replaced by Ballard in practice.

questions.question: While observing free play, a nurse sees a 3-year-old squeezing and shaping a lump of clay between the fingers and palms. This behaviour illustrates which fine motor accomplishment?
questions.explanation: Kneading and moulding a soft material calls for a mature pincer grasp combined with in-hand palmar manipulation and bilateral coordination, which is exactly the level of fine motor control typical of a 3-year-old. It is the behaviour set out in the scenario.

explanations.A: Spontaneous scribbling appears much earlier, around 15 to 18 months, and imitation of a vertical stroke by about 2 years. It is not what the child in the scenario is doing.
explanations.B: A tower of six cubes is expected at about 24 months and eight to nine cubes by roughly 30 months. Stacking is a different manipulative skill from moulding and is not described here.
explanations.C: Kneading and moulding a soft material calls for a mature pincer grasp combined with in-hand palmar manipulation and bilateral coordination, which is exactly the level of fine motor control typical of a 3-year-old. It is the behaviour set out in the scenario.
explanations.D: Copying a circle is indeed a 3-year milestone, but the question asks which skill the child is demonstrating, and no drawing is taking place.

questions.question: A baby is born with a fluid-filled sac protruding over the lower back; there is no bleeding into it and no clinical evidence of infection. If cerebrospinal fluid were sampled, what would the analysis most likely show?
questions.explanation: In a meningocele the defect contains only meninges and cerebrospinal fluid; the spinal cord and nerve roots stay within the canal. With the sac intact and uninfected the fluid retains normal cell count, protein, glucose and pressure. This is also why neurological function is usually preserved, in contrast to myelomeningocele.

explanations.A: Pleocytosis would mean meningitis, a recognised complication when the sac leaks or ruptures, but the scenario specifically excludes infection.
explanations.B: In a meningocele the defect contains only meninges and cerebrospinal fluid; the spinal cord and nerve roots stay within the canal. With the sac intact and uninfected the fluid retains normal cell count, protein, glucose and pressure. This is also why neurological function is usually preserved, in contrast to myelomeningocele.
explanations.C: Red cells in the fluid would indicate haemorrhage into the sac or a traumatic tap, neither of which is present.
explanations.D: A low cerebrospinal fluid glucose, typically under two-thirds of the blood value, is the hallmark of bacterial meningitis because organisms and inflammatory cells consume glucose. It has no reason to occur in an uncomplicated meningocele.

questions.citation: Ghai Essential Pediatrics 9e — neural tube defects

questions.question: A newborn with myelomeningocele is kept under close watch for a rise in intracranial pressure. Which change at the anterior fontanelle would support that suspicion?
questions.explanation: Most babies with myelomeningocele develop hydrocephalus, frequently on the basis of an associated Arnold-Chiari II malformation. As cerebrospinal fluid accumulates the anterior fontanelle becomes full, tense and bulging when the infant is held upright and settled, and it is accompanied by separation of the cranial sutures, a head circumference crossing centiles, dilated scalp veins, the 'setting sun' eye sign, a high-pitched cry, vomiting and irritability.

explanations.A: A depressed fontanelle points the other way, towards volume depletion from dehydration, and is accompanied by dry mucosa, reduced skin turgor and poor urine output.
explanations.B: A soft, flat fontanelle that pulsates normally when the baby is quiet and upright is a reassuring finding and argues against raised pressure.
explanations.C: Most babies with myelomeningocele develop hydrocephalus, frequently on the basis of an associated Arnold-Chiari II malformation. As cerebrospinal fluid accumulates the anterior fontanelle becomes full, tense and bulging when the infant is held upright and settled, and it is accompanied by separation of the cranial sutures, a head circumference crossing centiles, dilated scalp veins, the 'setting sun' eye sign, a high-pitched cry, vomiting and irritability.
explanations.D: The anterior fontanelle normally closes between 12 and 18 months. Premature closure suggests craniosynostosis and is not a marker of acutely raised pressure in the newborn.

questions.question: The parents of a 5-year-old with asthma are being taught about a metered-dose inhaler of Asthalin (salbutamol), 2 puffs to be taken every 6 hours. Which instruction matters most?
options: Administer only during acute asthma attacks
Use a spacer device for effective delivery
Increase to 4 puffs if symptoms worsen
questions.explanation: A young child cannot reliably coordinate actuation with a slow deep inhalation and cannot hold the breath for ten seconds. A valved holding chamber removes the need for that timing, lets the child breathe tidally through it for five to six breaths, cuts the high-velocity oropharyngeal impaction and roughly doubles the drug reaching the lower airway. Below 5 years the spacer is fitted with a face mask; above that a mouthpiece is used, and rinsing the mouth afterwards is still advised.

explanations.A: The drug has been prescribed on a fixed six-hourly schedule, so restricting it to attacks contradicts the order. Salbutamol can be used both as scheduled relief and as rescue medication.
explanations.B: A young child cannot reliably coordinate actuation with a slow deep inhalation and cannot hold the breath for ten seconds. A valved holding chamber removes the need for that timing, lets the child breathe tidally through it for five to six breaths, cuts the high-velocity oropharyngeal impaction and roughly doubles the drug reaching the lower airway. Below 5 years the spacer is fitted with a face mask; above that a mouthpiece is used, and rinsing the mouth afterwards is still advised.
explanations.C: Doubling the dose on the family's own initiative masks deteriorating control and delays medical review; excess beta-2 stimulation also brings tremor, tachycardia and hypokalaemia. Escalation belongs in a written action plan agreed with the clinician.
explanations.D: Inhaled salbutamol acts locally on airway smooth muscle and its absorption is not influenced by food, so linking doses to mealtimes serves no purpose.

questions.question: An infant aged 14 days is brought to the unit with rapid breathing, irritability and reluctance to feed. What should the nurse do first?
options: Perform a complete clinical assessment and check for jaundice or signs of infection
Advise the mother to increase breastfeeding frequency
questions.explanation: Assessment is the first step of the nursing process, and the IMNCI young-infant algorithm is built on exactly this: count the respiratory rate over a full minute (60 or more per minute is fast breathing at this age), record temperature, look for severe chest indrawing, grunting, convulsions, lethargy, movement only on stimulation, umbilical redness, skin pustules and the extent of jaundice, and take a feeding history. The pattern described is consistent with possible serious bacterial infection, and the findings gathered here determine whether the infant is classified for urgent referral.

explanations.A: Treatment cannot precede assessment, and in any case a young infant with suspected serious bacterial infection needs parenteral, not oral, antibiotics together with referral. Which antibiotic and by what route can only be decided after the child has been examined.
explanations.B: Assessment is the first step of the nursing process, and the IMNCI young-infant algorithm is built on exactly this: count the respiratory rate over a full minute (60 or more per minute is fast breathing at this age), record temperature, look for severe chest indrawing, grunting, convulsions, lethargy, movement only on stimulation, umbilical redness, skin pustules and the extent of jaundice, and take a feeding history. The pattern described is consistent with possible serious bacterial infection, and the findings gathered here determine whether the infant is classified for urgent referral.
explanations.C: Phototherapy is started against a measured serum or transcutaneous bilirubin plotted on an age- and risk-specific chart, never on impression alone. It would also leave the more urgent possibility of sepsis untreated.
explanations.D: Poor feeding in a two-week-old is a danger sign to be investigated, not a supply problem to be corrected with counselling. Feeding advice is appropriate only once serious illness has been excluded.

questions.question: Oxygen at 50 percent concentration is running at high flow for a 4-year-old. How should the delivered gas best be humidified?
options: Use a dry oxygen delivery system
Provide intermittent humidification with a heated humidifier
Use a cold mist humidifier continuously
questions.explanation: A heated humidifier is the appropriate device whenever flows are high or oxygen is given for more than a short period. Warming the water to near body temperature allows the gas to carry far more water vapour than a cold bubble system can, so it arrives at close to body temperature and full saturation, keeping the mucosa intact and secretions mobile. Water temperature and level are checked, condensate is drained away from the child, and the circuit is changed per unit policy to limit bacterial growth.

explanations.A: Piped oxygen is anhydrous. Delivered dry at high flow it strips moisture from the airway lining, thickens secretions, paralyses ciliary clearance and causes nasal pain, epistaxis and mucus plugging — a particular hazard in the narrow airways of a small child.
explanations.B: A heated humidifier is the appropriate device whenever flows are high or oxygen is given for more than a short period. Warming the water to near body temperature allows the gas to carry far more water vapour than a cold bubble system can, so it arrives at close to body temperature and full saturation, keeping the mucosa intact and secretions mobile. Water temperature and level are checked, condensate is drained away from the child, and the circuit is changed per unit policy to limit bacterial growth.
explanations.C: Hourly saline nebulisation is not a humidification strategy. It delivers repeated fluid boluses to the airway, may trigger bronchospasm and interrupts the continuity of oxygen delivery.
explanations.D: A cold or bubble humidifier adds relatively little water vapour because cool gas holds less moisture, so it is inadequate for high-flow oxygen; cold aerosol can also provoke bronchospasm in a child with irritable airways.

questions.question: Phototherapy is begun for a 3-day-old whose serum bilirubin measures 15 mg/dL. If effective phototherapy lowers the level by 1–2 mg/dL in every 4–6 hour period, what value should be anticipated at 12 hours?
questions.explanation: Twelve hours spans two intervals at the 6-hour end and three at the 4-hour end. Multiplying by a fall of 1 to 2 mg/dL per interval gives a total drop of roughly 3 to 6 mg/dL, so 15 mg/dL should come down to about 9 to 12 mg/dL. This range covers both the slowest and the fastest plausible response and is therefore the best estimate.

explanations.A: A final value of 12 to 13 mg/dL means a fall of only 2 to 3 mg/dL over the whole 12 hours, which is what one interval alone would achieve and understates the expected response.
explanations.B: Twelve hours spans two intervals at the 6-hour end and three at the 4-hour end. Multiplying by a fall of 1 to 2 mg/dL per interval gives a total drop of roughly 3 to 6 mg/dL, so 15 mg/dL should come down to about 9 to 12 mg/dL. This range covers both the slowest and the fastest plausible response and is therefore the best estimate.
explanations.C: A reading of 13 to 14 mg/dL represents a fall of just 1 to 2 mg/dL. Such a poor response after 12 hours would prompt a check of irradiance, lamp distance and skin exposure, and a search for ongoing haemolysis.
explanations.D: A fall to 10 to 11 mg/dL does sit inside the possible band, but it is too narrow an answer: it excludes both the slower 3 mg/dL and the faster 6 mg/dL ends of the calculated range.

questions.question: A preterm baby in the NICU is being watched for hypoxia. Of the manifestations listed, which one appears LATE in the course?
questions.explanation: Cyanosis is a late and unreliable sign. Visible blue discolouration requires roughly 5 g/dL of desaturated haemoglobin in the capillary bed, so it appears only after oxygenation has fallen substantially, and it can be masked altogether in an anaemic infant or exaggerated in polycythaemia. Central cyanosis of the tongue and mucous membranes is the significant form; peripheral acrocyanosis in the first day or two of life is normal. Pulse oximetry and blood gases detect the problem long before the colour changes.

explanations.A: A rise in respiratory rate is one of the first compensatory responses, driven by chemoreceptor stimulation as oxygen tension falls.
explanations.B: Flaring of the alae nasi, along with retractions and grunting, is early accessory-muscle work aimed at reducing airway resistance and increasing tidal volume.
explanations.C: Cyanosis is a late and unreliable sign. Visible blue discolouration requires roughly 5 g/dL of desaturated haemoglobin in the capillary bed, so it appears only after oxygenation has fallen substantially, and it can be masked altogether in an anaemic infant or exaggerated in polycythaemia. Central cyanosis of the tongue and mucous membranes is the significant form; peripheral acrocyanosis in the first day or two of life is normal. Pulse oximetry and blood gases detect the problem long before the colour changes.
explanations.D: Restlessness and irritability reflect early cerebral hypoxia, later giving way to lethargy and reduced responsiveness as the deficit deepens.

questions.question: Parents are being prepared to take home an infant who is fed through a jejunostomy tube. Which point should the nurse stress in the discharge teaching?
options: Administer high-calorie formula orally to promote weight gain
Monitor the jejunostomy site daily for signs of infection or leakage
Clean the jejunostomy tube with alcohol-based solution twice daily
Restrict fluid intake to prevent excessive output from the jejunostomy
questions.explanation: Daily inspection of the exit site is the cornerstone of home care. Parents are taught to look for redness, swelling, warmth, discharge, excoriated skin, granulation tissue and leakage of feed around the tube, to keep the site clean and dry, to check the external marking so displacement is recognised, and to report any of these promptly. Leaking jejunal contents rapidly erode the surrounding skin, and a dislodged tube is an emergency because the tract closes quickly.

explanations.A: A jejunostomy is placed precisely because the oral or gastric route is unsafe or inadequate. Nutrition goes through the tube, usually as a continuous or slow intermittent infusion since the jejunum cannot handle bolus volumes; any oral intake is introduced only on the team's advice.
explanations.B: Daily inspection of the exit site is the cornerstone of home care. Parents are taught to look for redness, swelling, warmth, discharge, excoriated skin, granulation tissue and leakage of feed around the tube, to keep the site clean and dry, to check the external marking so displacement is recognised, and to report any of these promptly. Leaking jejunal contents rapidly erode the surrounding skin, and a dislodged tube is an emergency because the tract closes quickly.
explanations.C: Alcohol dehydrates and irritates peristomal skin and can degrade the tube material. Mild soap and water, dried well, is the recommended routine.
explanations.D: Withholding fluid in an infant on jejunal feeding invites dehydration and electrolyte disturbance. High output is managed by adjusting the rate, concentration or formula composition, and by replacing losses, not by limiting what the child receives.
